passages.text: As mentioned before, CSF2 and IFN-gamma induce the expression of IRF5, which activates M1 macrophages and inhibits M2 macrophages. Furthermore, CSF2R participates in the repolarization of M2 macrophages towards an M1 phenotype. The upregulation of the suppressor of cytokine signalling (SOCS) 3 suppressor through STAT1/STAT2 is also crucial for the efficient activation of M1 macrophages. A study by Arnold et al. showed that SOCS3 expression regulates phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) activity, favors nitrogen (II) oxide (NO) production, and leads to the activation and translocation of Nuclear-kappa B factor (NF-kappaB). Furthermore, activin A has been observed to promote the expression of the typical markers of M1 macrophages by negatively regulating IL-10 production, likely leading to M1 polarization.

On the other hand, CSF1, TGF-beta, interleukins: 4, 6, 13, 10, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), released by tumor cells, can cause macrophage polarization into M2 macrophages. Other molecules, involved in M2 polarization, are IRF4, which is a negative controller of TLR signaling associated with the MyD88 adaptor molecule, or NFkappaB. Furthermore, Ohmori et al. showed that IL-4 inhibits IFN-gamma-stimulated gene transcription and increases STAT6 activation, affecting arginase 1(Arg1) production by M2 macrophages. On the other hand, IL-21 influences polarization in M2 macrophages by inhibiting extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation and reducing inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), which in turn increases STAT3 phosphorylation. Furthermore, the complement 32 response gene (RGC-32), which is a cell cycle regulator, also plays an important role in the polarization of M2 macrophages. The factors presented influence the phenotype of macrophages, which varies depending on the stimuli they receive. Some of these factors are present in TME and are involved in the development of specific macrophages that participate, e.g., in tumor growth.
3. Tumor-Associated Macrophages (TAMs)
3.1. Characteristics of TAMs

Macrophages are relocated to tumor areas and differentiate into TAMs in response to various cytokines, such as IL-34, CSF1, members of VEGFs, and chemokines, such as CCL5 and CCL2. The TME influences the secretion of cytokines, chemokines, and other agents released by mesenchymal cells, tumor cells, or immune cells. These factors, in the presence of inflammation, local hypoxia, and high levels of lactic acid, cause the relocation of monocytes from blood into the TME and repolarize them into a particular type of macrophage, called a TAM. TAMs are more polarized towards M2 macrophages, which refers to more aggressive tumor hallmarks, represented by tumor invasion, progression, and metastasis. The polarization of TAMs into the pro-tumor phenotype can also be caused by dying cancer cells. For example, apoptotic cells release sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), which attracts and activates TAMs by reducing IL-12 production and downregulating MHC-II expression. Necrotic cells, on the other hand, can promote tumor growth by recruiting TAMs to the TME and releasing IL-1alpha.

Although TAMs are more similar to M2 macrophages, they have both M1 and M2 polarity signatures. In response to different stimulants, TAMs can differentiate into separate functional subgroups. Th1 T cells (by secreting IFN-gamma, TNF-alpha, LPS, etc.) lead TAMs to transform into M1 macrophages, and Th2 T cells (by secreting TGFbeta1, IL-10, IL-4, PGE2, etc.) transform them into M2 macrophages. Therefore, TAMs express both M1 and M2 markers, such as MGL1, CD81, MHC-II, SR-A, PD-L1, CD163, MRC1, CD206, CD204 etc..
3.2. TAMs Function in Tumor Development

TAMs influence both the TME and tumor cells (Figure 1). In the TME, TAMs secrete various cytokines, chemokines, and enzymes, such as, e.g., TGF-beta, prostaglandins, IL-10, CCL22, CCL17, galectin-3 (Gal-3), and metalloproteinases (MMP), that induce immunosuppression by the activation of regulatory T cells (TREG), which, in consequence, lead to the loss of T cell function to recognize and kill tumor cells. TAMs can inhibit cytotoxic CD8+ T cells by the metabolic starvation of T cells through the secretion of immunosuppressive metabolites (i.e., NO, ROS). Many other suppressive markers, interacting with tumor cells, are observed in TAM, such as, for example, (1) programmed death cell receptor 1 (PD-1), a PD-L1 ligand in tumor cells; (2) CD80, a CD28/cytotoxic T lymphocyte Associated Protein 4 (CTLA-4) ligand; (3) V-domain Ig suppressor of T cell activation (VISTA); (4) signal regulatory protein alpha (SIRPA), a ligand for the CD47 receptor; (5) leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor subfamily B member 1 (LILRB1), an MHC-I ligand; or (6) sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectin 10 (Siglec-10), a CD24 ligand. The PD-1/PD-L1 signalling pathway enhances tumor immune escape by inhibiting macrophage normal function and binding Siglec-10 to CD24. In addition, it limits the functions of T effector cells, NK cells, and dendritic cells (including the suppression of activation, proliferation, and cytokine expression). On the other hand, The SIRPA/CD47 pathway is defined as the signal 'do not eat me', which recognizes CD47-expressing tumor cells as self-normal cells and results in the inhibition of phagocytosis. LILRB1, located on the surface of macrophages, is recognized by MHC-I molecules and changes macrophage function from tumor growth inhibition to tumor promotion. In addition, vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1, CD106), which mediates TAM adhesion to the vascular endothelium, is expressed in TAMs.

annotations.text: leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor subfamily B member 1

passages.text: In addition to the modulation of the TME, TAMs promote tumor development and progression by releasing factors that enhance tumor growth, invasion, angiogenesis, and metastasis potential. Many cytokines released by TAMs are involved in tumor growth. For example, through IL-6 secretion, TAMs increase the capacity for carcinogenesis and tumor progression by controlling genes related to the cell cycle, angiogenesis, inflammation, and stem cell self-renewal promotion. IL-6 participates in the STAT3 signaling pathway, promoting tumorigenesis and the induction of cancer stem cells (CSCs). In tumor development are also involved other factors secreted by TAMs, eg IL-10, that support tumor growth and aggressiveness through the PI3K signaling pathway and the Janus-Activated Kinase (JAK)1/STAT1/NF-kB/neurogenic locus homolog protein 1 (Notch1) pathway, or CCL2, which activates the PI3K/protein kinase B (Akt)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR). Furthermore, the CSF2 receptor (CSF2R) in TAMs is involved in the regulation of JAK2/STAT3/5, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), NFkappaB, and PI3K signaling pathways.

In addition, TAMs also support angiogenesis. In these processes, the key roles are of VEGFs in promoting the vascularization process, and MMPs in promoting the degradation of the extracellular matrix (ECM). Furthermore, tumor angiogenesis is encouraged by the IL-1beta, IL-8, TNF-alpha, PDGF, and basic bFGF, secreted by TAMs. VEGFs and MMPs are also involved in tumor invasion. This process is related to the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which can be mediated by the secretion of IL-6 and TGF-beta, through the JAK/STAT3/Snail and Smad/Snail pathways, respectively. EMT can also be induced by epidermal growth factor (EGF) secretion, activating the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-ERK signaling pathway. MMPs, EGF, and CSF-1 factors enhance cell migration and are involved in metastasis. Furthermore, tumor metastasis is supported by IL-8 secretion through the upregulation of engulfment and cell motility 1 (ELMO1) expression, a tumor-expressed protein involved in cell migration, phagocytosis, and morphological changes.
4. TAMs in Sarcomas
4.1. TAMs Phenotype and Role in Sarcoma

TAMs have been widely identified among sarcomas. They have been found in STS (in 90%, in a study of various types of sarcomas, including 14 gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), five synovial sarcomas (SSs), four leiomyosarcomas (LMSs), and one-three cases of 18 other types). In addition, they have also been identified in bone sarcomas (e.g., osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma (ES), and chondrosarcoma). The TAMs presented in STS and bone sarcomas have various markers identified on their surface (Figure 2).

One of these markers is SIRPA, which is a glycoprotein of the SIRP family, located mainly on the membrane of myeloid cells, but it is also identified on the surface of macrophages, including TAMs. It has been identified in both STS and bone sarcoma. In macrophages, SIRPA recognizes CD47, which negatively regulates the effector function of innate immunity cells, such as the phagocytosis of the host, and participates in homeostasis processes by removing dying cells. The inhibition of phagocytic potency against tumor cells is also caused by the expression of PD-1 in TAMs. PD-1 expression has been observed in the human osteosarcoma mouse model and patient samples of osteosarcoma with lung metastases. In this study, anti-PD1 antibodies led to a decrease in the number of tumor cells and enhanced tumor apoptosis by blocking the p-STAT3/p-Erk1/2 signaling pathway. Furthermore, an increased number of M1 macrophages and NK cells was observed after PD-1 blockade.

The following marker is the tyrosine kinase receptor CSF1R, expressed in circulating monocytes and macrophages, which is a ligand for CSF1 and IL-34. These factors are secreted by tumor cells and cause the recruitment of TAMs. CSF1 is highly expressed in several types of solid tumors, and in addition to recruiting peripheral blood monocytes to the TME, it plays a role in the differentiation of monocytes into macrophages. Furthermore, CSF1 participates in polarization to an M2-like phenotype by binding to CSF1R. In a study by Fujiwara et al., the in vitro administration of Pexidartinib (PLX3397) reduced TAM M2-like polarization to an M1-like phenotype with a simultaneous decrease in forkhead box P3 (FOXP3)+ regulatory T cells and the increased migration of CD8+ T cells. Moreover, in the same study, in the osteosarcoma mice model, PLX3397 administration suppressed the primary tumor growth and lung metastasis in vivo. On the other hand, IL-34 induces the adhesion of monocytes to endothelial cells, improving the migration capacity of TAMs, which was observed in osteosarcoma. Sarcoma cells may also secrete the macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) pleiotropic cytokine, which interacts with the CD74 receptor, expressed in macrophages, and translates their phenotype into pro-tumoral, as it was observed in in vitro and in vivo studies in the STS mouse model.

On the other hand, CCL22, IL-10, TGF-beta, and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) 1, secreted by TAMs, lead to immunosuppression, resulting in the inhibition of effector T cells and TREG activation. One of them, IDO1, is a principal regulator of the tryptophan (Trp) catabolism pathway, leading to the loss of antitumor immunity and tumor growth. Kynurenine, produced by IDO1, promotes the selective expansion of Tregs. In this process, the PD-L1 and CD80 receptors are also involved, leading to T-cell dysfunction. For example, in a preclinical model of osteosarcoma, the inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction has been associated with antitumor activity.

Factors secreted by TAMs may also influence tumor growth in sarcomas, e.g., pro-inflammatory cytokines are specifically implicated in the pathogenesis of chondrosarcoma and osteosarcoma. For example, increased TNF-alpha, MMP-12, and MMP-13 expression were observed in chondrosarcoma cells during malignant transformation. However, MMP-9 increased the metastatic potential in osteosarcoma. Another factor, TGF-beta, has a key role in human chondrosarcoma migration and metastasis, for example, by increasing human chondrosarcoma mobility through the PI3K/Akt pathway. TAMs may also promote invasiveness by secreting CCL18 and pro-inflammatory molecules, such as cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2), which were observed in metastatic osteosarcoma. Furthermore, IL-6 promotes stemness in osteosarcoma by up-regulating the signaling pathway regulating EMT, through STAT3 phosphorylation. On the other hand, IL-34 has been reported to induce vasculogenesis and tumor growth in osteosarcoma through the activation of endothelial cell signaling pathways, including the proto-oncogene tyrosine protein kinase Src (Src), focal adhesion kinase (FAK), and MAPKs, involved in angiogenesis and vascular homeostasis. Furthermore, in osteosarcoma, TAMs promoted angiogenesis through the secretion of VEGF.

Other markers, characteristic of sarcoma TAMs, are CD163 and CD68, specific for M2 and M1 macrophages, respectively. They were commonly observed among sarcomas, for example, in chondrosarcoma and osteosarcoma or angiosarcoma, and dedifferentiated liposarcoma. In a study by Burns et al., a poor correlation between CD163 and STAT6 was found in dedifferentiated liposarcoma and in undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (UPS). A study by Handl et al. of 24 patients with primary ES has shown that CD163 is a sensitive marker for macrophages in this group of sarcomas, although it lacks specificity for the M2 phenotype.

Other M2-like TAMs, identified in sarcomas, are, for example, mannose receptor-1 (MMR, CD206), observed in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP), and osteosarcoma, macrophage scavenger receptor 1 (MSR1, CD204), observed in UPS, and dendritic cell-specific ICAM-3 capture non-integrin (DC-SIGN, CD209) and melanoma cell adhesion molecule (MCAM, CD146), observed in osteosarcoma. Moreover, in a study by Jiang et al., the expression of structural maintenance of chromosomes 4 (SMC4) was significantly correlated with CD14+ and CSF1R+ monocytes, CD80+ TAMs, prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2 (PTGS2)+ M1 macrophages, and the expression of depleted CTLA4+ T cells. This suggests that SMC4 may play a role in regulating the infiltration and activity of TAM and T cell function inhibition and, therefore, may promote the development of sarcoma.

In the study by Dancsok et al., in a cohort of patients with approximately 960 cases of sarcomas (including STSs: DFSP, extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EMC), UPS, GIST, low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma (LGFMS), LMS, myxofibrosarcoma (MFS), malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), epithelioid sarcoma, alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS), SS, angiosarcoma, liposarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, clear cell sarcoma; and bone sarcomas: chondrosarcoma, chordoma, osteosarcoma, ES), among almost all analyzed cases, TAMs outnumbered the tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs). The same observation was made in a study by Fan et al. of 472 samples with eight different diagnosed sarcomas (including 123 osteosarcomas and 211 STS, such as ES, fibrosarcoma, LMS, liposarcoma, SS, UPS, etc.), where two of the most common fractions of immune cells were M2 macrophages (almost 34%) and nonactivated macrophages (M0) (around 21%). In another cohort, including 253 localized STSs and GISTs, among many immune cells, the highest reported levels were of monocytes/macrophages.

Several markers of TAMs have already been described among different subtypes of sarcomas. One such marker is CD168. The high infiltration (85%) of CD168+ TAMs was observed, e.g., in dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, exclusively in dedifferentiated areas, and not in the well-differentiated component of chondrosarcoma. In a study by Richer et al., TAMs appeared to be the most abundant immune population both in the peritumoral area of conventional chondrosarcomas and in the dedifferentiated areas of dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas, compared to TILs (25% were CD163+ TAMs in conventional and 50% in dedifferentiated, compared to, respectively, 10% and 15% being CD3+ cells, and 8% and 5% being CD8+ cells). CD163+ macrophages were also identified in another cohort of 26 grade 1-3 conventional chondrosarcomas and were localized mainly at the peripheral site of the tumor. On the other hand, in osteosarcoma, CD14+HLA-DR+ M1 macrophages and CD14+CD163+ M2 macrophages were observed. Furthermore, in another study, a heterogenic population of TAMs with the phenotype of both M1 and M2 macrophages in osteosarcomas was identified. M2-like TAMs induced resistance to chemotherapy in primary osteosarcoma cells, by releasing IL-1beta, which in response caused the overexpression of IL-34, vasculogenesis, and osteosarcoma growth.

However, the CD163 marker has also been identified in STS. In a study of 134 adults with high-grade LMS, liposarcomas, and SS, a high number of CD163+ TAMs was identified in 49% of all cases and were correlated with the tumor grade in 53% of high-grade and 28% of low-grade tumors. However, the CD168+ TAM distribution was higher in LMS (66%), compared to liposarcoma and SS (respectively, 46% and 9%). The researchers also observed that STSs and bone sarcomas have a higher number of M2-like TAMs (marked with the CD163 marker) than M1-like TAMs. The M2: (M0+ M1) ratio was also higher in sarcomas without translocations, although SS was prone to have more M0 than M2 macrophages. Furthermore, GISTs, LMSs, and UPSs were noticeably infiltrated by CD163+ macrophages expressing IDO1.

Another marker, CD68, was particularly prominent among translocation-free sarcomas, especially pleomorphic liposarcoma, chordoma, chondrosarcoma (conventional and dedifferentiated subtypes), UPS, and angiosarcoma. These sarcomas had a significantly higher CD68: TIL ratio than translocation-associated sarcomas, which was confirmed by immunohistochemistry and the analysis of mRNA expression. Furthermore, in a validated cohort of 27 conventional and 49 dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas, a low expression of CD68+ TAMs was identified in approximately 39% of the patients, while its high expression was found in almost 61%.

The other TAM marker, SIRPA, was identified in macrophages in 31% of the sarcomas, especially chordoma (71% of the cases), dedifferentiated liposarcoma (77%), angiosarcoma (75%), and well-differentiated liposarcoma (65%). SIRPA+ TAM infiltration in osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma was less common (respectively, observed in around 30% and 2% of all cases). SIRPA+ TAMs were observed in both conventional and dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma. In all of these sarcomas, the expression of the SIRPA receptor was poorly correlated with the expression of CD47 in tumors. Furthermore, the expression of CD47 and SIRPA showed poor positive correlations with CD68+ and CD163+ macrophages in almost all sarcomas, except a solitary fibrous tumor, demonstrating a significant negative correlation between CD163+ and CD68+ TAMs, and CD47. SIRPA was also positively correlated with PD-L1 expression in TAMs in osteosarcoma, myxofibrosarcoma, dedifferentiated liposarcoma, and SS.

On the other hand, CSF1R expression was observed in STSs with complex genomic profiles and chondrosarcoma. In chondrosarcoma, the expression of CSF1R was involved in macrophage survival and proliferation and varied between conventional and dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma (64% of the conventional chondrosarcomas, and around 85% of the dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas were positive for CSF1R). CSF1R+ macrophages were found in the peripheral areas of grade 2 and 3 chondrosarcomas and in the dedifferentiated compartment of dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas.

In addition to the TAM markers mentioned above, in a study by Han et al., patients with aggressive pediatric bone sarcomas showed an increased number of peripheral CD14+ HLA-DR low/immunosuppressive monocytes and CTLA-4+ T cells, as well as CD14+ macrophage infiltrates. The presence of CD14+CD68+ M1 macrophages was also observed in a study of primary malignant bone tumors. Furthermore, in a cohort of 253 localized STSs and GISTs, the TAMs also expressed CD16a as well as CSF1R, CD163, and CD68. Another less common marker, described in TAMs, was the ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba1), observed in UPS.

The distribution of TAMs among sarcomas is very heterogeneous, as a group of tumors. For this reason, there is still not much known about the specific markers of TAMs and their interaction in sarcomas. This may impact the clinical relevance of TAMs and their conflicting function on clinical outcomes among different subtypes of sarcomas.
4.2. The Role of TAMs as a Predictive and Prognostic Factors in Sarcoma

The high infiltration of TAMs in TME is generally associated with a poor overall survival (OS) rate and metastasis in STS and bone sarcomas (Table 2). For example, a high infiltration of CD68+ TAMs tended to be associated with worse overall survival in the dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma with the osteosarcoma compartment, and the CD68/CD8 ratio was identified as an independent weak prognostic factor of OS in these patients. Furthermore, all patients with metastasis at diagnosis had higher levels of CD68+ and CD163+ TAMs. CD68+ TAMs were also an adverse prognostic factor that predicted a lower OS in ES, and worse progression-free survival (PFS) in LMS. Furthermore, higher levels of CD68+ TAMs were associated with a poorer OS in myxoid liposarcoma that promoted invasiveness through the heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HB-EGF)-EGFR-PI3K/Akt pathway. A study of almost 200 STSs indicated that CD68+ macrophages were independently associated with an increased risk of LR, regardless of margin status, age, sex, or the number of CD20+ B cells. CD68+ and CD163+ TAMs were related to worse disease-specific survival (DSS) in non-gynecologic LMS, while they were not associated with DSS in gynecologic LMS.

Furthermore, the highest CD163+ M2 macrophage density was found in the highest grade of chondrosarcoma, suggesting the involvement of M2 macrophages in tumor progression through its role in angiogenesis, migration, or invasion. In a study by Dancsok et al., solitary fibrous tumors with CD163+ macrophages had a worse prognosis (with lower PFS). Other studies revealed that CD14+, CD68+, and CD163+ macrophages were associated with a poor OS in myxoid liposarcoma and dedifferentiated liposarcoma. CD163+ macrophages were also associated with a worse OS and PFS in SS and with a poor OS in UPS. Furthermore, in a study by Schroeder et al., of 147 patients with sarcoma treated with trabectedin (including UPS, LMS, well-/dedifferentiated liposarcoma, SS, and uterine LMS), the gene signatures of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and M2 macrophages, and the high expression of M2 macrophages were significantly associated with a high death risk in the 7-year OS. In a study of 75 STS cases, a high number of CD68+, CD163+, and CD204+ macrophages in both the intratumoral and marginal areas was associated with worse disease-free survival (DFS); however, after the division of this group into grade 1 and grade 2/3, only in the grade 2/3 group were high numbers of CD163+ and CD204+ macrophages associated with poor DFS, and only in the marginal area.

Similarly, SIRPA+ and CSF1R+ TAMs were related to the metastatic status at diagnosis and a poor OS in patients with dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma. Furthermore, the appearance of SIRPalpha+ macrophages was also an adverse prognostic agent in both SS and myxofibrosarcoma, and it was associated with a worse OS in sarcomas without translocations. In UPS, in addition to CD163+ M2 macrophages, CD204+ M2 macrophages were associated with a worse OS. Among other markers, in osteosarcoma, TAMs expressing CD47 predicted an inferior PFS.

However, TAMs can have also a positive prognostic role in some cases (Table 2). A study by Handl et al., has shown an association between the CD163 expression of TAMs and a lower stage of ES. A higher presence of CD163+ macrophages was associated with localized disease and a longer OS. The same results were obtained in osteosarcoma, where CD163+ macrophages were significantly correlated with CD146+ and macrophage activation factor (cMAF)+ macrophages and were associated with a higher OS rate. In dedifferentiated liposarcoma and LMS, a high infiltration of CD163+ TAMs was a prognostic factor with a longer PFS.
Summary of various tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and their clinical relevance among sarcomas.

Opposite results were obtained in the preclinical models of osteosarcoma, in which CD163+ M2 macrophages were correlated with tumor growth, vascularization, and metastasis. Due to the heterogeneity of sarcomas and the dual role of TAMs as prognostic factors, there is a huge need for further research in this field to better understand TAM phenotype and their mechanism of action among each sarcoma subtype.
5. Macrophages as Treatment Targets in Sarcoma

Due to the variety of functions of TAMs and their clinical significance, they have become a therapeutic target among STS and bone sarcomas. Currently, several clinical trials using monocytes and TAMs as the target in sarcomas are ongoing (Table 3). Targeted therapies using TAMs can be divided into those aimed at reducing macrophage recruitment, the repolarization of TAMs into antitumor, targeting activated TAMs, or causing the activation of phagocytosis.

TLR agonists have been used to assess macrophage polarization toward M1 activation status. One of these agents is muramyl tripeptide-phosphatidylethanolamine encapsulated in liposomes (L-MTP-PE, Mifamurtide, Mepact , London, UK), which has been suggested as an adjuvant therapy for patients with osteosarcoma. Mifamurtide stimulates the response of the immune system by binding to nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 2 (NOD2) in an intracellular receptor molecule, expressed in monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. L-MTP-PE has been shown to cause TLR4 activation in macrophages and monocytes. In addition, it can upregulate the pro-tumor functions of macrophages by increasing cytokine production (such as TNF-alpha, NO, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12). In phase II clinical trials, L-MTP-PE was found to cause the infiltration of activated macrophages into lung tissue in osteosarcoma metastases. On the other hand, in a follow-up randomized phase III trial [Intergroup (INT)-0133] involving patients with osteosarcoma, the supplement of L-MTP-PE to standard chemotherapy did not demonstrate differences in the 5-year OS or event-free survival (EFS). However, L-MTP-PE improved the 5-year OS and EFS in patients with metastatic disease, compared to those who did not receive L-MTP-PE (53 vs. 40% OS and 46% vs. 26% EFS). Punzo et al., showed that L-MTP-PE may modulate macrophage functions, with the inhibition of osteosarcoma cell proliferation by switching macrophage polarity to TAM with an intermediate M1/M2 phenotype. A preclinical evaluation of L-MTP-PE in combination with zoledronic acid (ZA) in osteosarcoma murine models also has shown that these two drugs significantly suppress tumor growth and the development of metastatic disease. Other potential agents involved in TAM repolarization that were tested in preclinical models in OS models were all-trans-retinoic acid, asiaticoside, Resiquimod (R848), and esculetin.

PLX3397 (Turalio ; Daiichi Sankyo, Inc., Tokyo, Japan), which is a CSF1/CSF1R inhibitor and agent that changes macrophage polarization, was tested in sarcomas in numerous clinical trials (NCT01004861, NCT01525602, NCT02390752, and NCT02584647). Preclinical studies have demonstrated that the CSF1/CSF1R signaling cascade reduces the number of infiltrating TAMs and causes M2 to M1 repolarization. PLX3397 has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in the treatment of unresectable tenosynovial giant cell tumors, and, currently, together with sirolimus, is being examined in a phase I/II trial for unresectable sarcomas (such as ES, liposarcoma, LMS, MPNST, SS and rhabdomyosarcoma) (NCT02584647).

passages.text: Imatinib (STI571, Glivec ; Novartis AG, Basel, Switzerland) is a strong and selective inhibitor of several tyrosine kinases, including platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), which is the therapeutic option for patients with GIST. Cavnar et al., indicated that TAMs in GISTs are similar to M1 macrophages at baseline; however, they become similar to M2 macrophages in response to the inhibition of the KIT (CD117) oncoprotein by imatinib treatment. As a result, KIT inhibition leads to tumor cell apoptosis, the down-regulation of M1 macrophages, and up-regulation of M2 markers, which then causes T cell inhibition and the dual consequence of this treatment. TAMs have been reported to be M1-like in untreated tumors; however, they change to M2-like in response to imatinib and eventually return to M1-like in imatinib-resistant GIST.

Another multikinase inhibitor, regorafenib, can induce antitumor activity by modulating macrophage polarization. It was observed in in vivo and in vitro liver cancer models by activating the p38MAPK/cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) responsive element binding protein 1 (Creb1)/Krupple-like factor 4 (Klf4) pathway after regorafenib administration. The randomized double-blind phase II study of the regorafenib in patients with metastatic osteosarcoma (NCT02048371) revealed that the median PFS was significantly improved with the regorafenib (3.6 months (95% CI, 2.0 to 7.6 months) versus 1.7 months (95% CI, 1.2 to 1.8 months) in the placebo group); however, there were no statistically significant differences in the OS of these groups.

Trabectedin (Yondelis ; PharmaMar, Madrid, Spain) is another potential agent in sarcoma treatment, which has been shown to activate a TNF-related apoptosis-inducing ligand (TRAIL) in TAMs and monocytes, and it is involved in the TRAIL/caspase 8-dependent pathway of apoptosis. TRAIL expression has been indicated, e.g., in the human ES cell line or murine fibrosarcoma cells. Trabectedin has recently been approved for the treatment of advanced STS, and it was reported to partially decrease circulating monocytes and TAMs in myxoid liposarcoma cells. Furthermore, Germano et al., also showed that trabectedin decreased the TAM density and reduced angiogenesis in human sarcoma cells.

Another strategy relies on blocking specific receptors in TAMs. One of these examples may be PD-1/PD-L1 signaling using, for example, pembrolizumab, a highly selective humanized monoclonal antibody. In a phase II study of four cohorts of patients with STS, including LMS, UPS, GIST, and others, patients received pembrolizumab combined with metronomic cyclophosphamide (NCT02406781). The results of the 6-month PFS rates were 0% for LMS and UPS, 11% for GIST, and 14% for others. Furthermore, in the same study, IDO1 was expressed mainly by macrophages in, respectively, 69%, 73%, 63%, and 29% of LMS, UPS, GIST, and others. Therefore, PD-1 inhibition has decreased activity in some GIST and STS, which may be explained by macrophage infiltration and activation of the IDO1 pathway, leading to immunosuppressive TME. Due to the negative correlation of PD-1 expression in TAMs with phagocytic capacity against tumor cells, macrophage-targeted therapy with immune checkpoint modification can be a target for directed therapies. The preclinical study showed that the combination of a CSF1R inhibitor with PD-1 or CTLA-4 antagonists induces tumor regression, compared to the single use of PD-1 or CTLA-4 inhibitors. However, the phase I/IIa clinical trial of PLX3397 for patients with advanced melanoma and other solid tumors was not continued due to unsatisfactory clinical efficiency (NCT02452424). On the other hand, a study by Edris et al. reported that the inhibition of CD47/SIRPA signaling may be another promising target in the future. In this study, CD47 inhibition increased the macrophage phagocytic capacity in two human LMS cell lines (LMS04 and LMS05) in vitro. Furthermore, it reduced the primary tumor size in a metastatic murine model of LMS.
6. Conclusions

TAMs are a specific group of immune cells in TME and have been widely indicated in many sarcomas, including both STSs (i.e., DFSP, EMC, LGFMS, MFS, MPNST, ASPS, epithelioid sarcoma, clear cell sarcoma, angiosarcoma, liposarcoma, SS, LMS, UPS, GIST, rhabdomyosarcoma, fibrosarcoma) and bone sarcomas (adult and pediatric osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, chordoma, ES). TAMs have a great impact on both the tumor and surrounding immune cells, such as T cells, NK cells, and other macrophages. TAMs participate in tumor migration and invasion, and lead to an immunosuppression mechanism in many subtypes of sarcomas, through the expression of several markers (PD-1, PD-L1, CD80, SIRPA, CD206, CD209, CD146, CD14, CD68, CD163, CSF1R, etc.) and the secretion of multiple cytokines (IL-10, IL-6, IL-8, CSF1, IL-34, TGF-beta, VEGF, etc.), chemokines (CCl2, CCL5, CCL18, CCL22, etc.) and other factors (such as MMP-9, COX2, and IDO1 etc.). In this process, various important pathways, including the JAK/MAPK, JAK/STAT3, p-STAT3/p-Erk1/2, and JAK/PI3K/AKT signaling pathways seem to be involved.

In addition, TAMs can be significant prognostic and predictive factors. They are generally related to a poor OS and the appearance of metastases among sarcomas, for example, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, liposarcoma, UPS, or LMS, especially TAMs with the expression of CD163, CD68, SIPRA, CD204, or CD206. On the other hand, in some sarcomas, e.g., ES or osteosarcoma, the infiltration of TAMs was a favorable prognostic or predictive factor. The variety of TAM function and their clinical significance have led to research on targeting TAMs, as potential therapeutics in the treatment of STS and bone sarcomas. Among them, therapies related to TAM repolarization, targeting activated TAMs, phagocytosis activation, and TLR antagonists are under development. Currently, Pexidartinib and Trabectedin are approved for sarcoma treatment; however, there are many ongoing clinical trials with other drug candidates.

In conclusion, there is still much to be discovered about TAMs and their role in the pathogenesis of different types of sarcomas and their impact on TME. Their impact on clinical outcomes is still unclear, which may be due to the heterogeneity of these tumors and their rare occurrence, making them a difficult target for research. However, TAMs appear to be a promising target for treatment due to their wide distribution among many subtypes of sarcoma and the presence of specific markers on their surface. Further studies are needed to better understand the mechanism of the repolarization of TAMs and their differential impact on clinical significance among sarcomas, which may lead to the development of effective targeted therapies using TAMs in the future.

DCs:dendritic cells, NK cells:natural killer cells.

Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and their impact on the microenvironment of sarcomas. TAMs display a pro-tumor phenotype with polarization toward M2-type macrophages. TAMs lead to modulation of tumor microenvironment (TME) by CD80/CTLA-4 and PD-1/PD-L1 interaction, secretion of MMP-9, COX2, IDO1, and several cytokines and chemokines e.g., IL-10, Il-34, IL-6, TGF-B, CSF1, VEGF. passages.text: Moving
Abstract

Examples of realized scientific careers can provide ideas and inspiration for others aiming to pursue such careers. Here I recount in brief the story of my long career in primatology (1973 to the present), focusing on one enduring theme in my research: the nature and genesis of goal-directed action (evident in movement). The story begins in graduate school, passes through developing my own laboratory, on to pursuing a spectrum of studies with mentees and collaborators, developing a theoretical explanatory framework for goal-directed action that I think holds promise for the field as a whole, and ends with an exciting field project that seems a suitable finale to my career. I mention the value to me, the field, and society of participation in scientific societies, including the American Society of Primatologists, throughout my career.

A career in primatology of a comparative psychologist/ethologist spans teaching, mentoring, university and professional service, and research: experimental and observational studies of primates, including studies of bearded capuchin monkeys cracking nuts with stone hammers and anvils (photo courtesy of Barth Wright).
Research Highlights
This review summarizes a primatologist's research journey from graduate school in the 1970s to the present.
Observational and experimental studies with animals in captive and natural settings weave together a complex picture of goal-directed action in primates.
Aspiring scientists and those new to the field may take inspiration from this story of one person's experience of following a big question with the help of many collaborators.
INTRODUCTION

"Move" is one of my favorite words. "To move" is a transitive, reflexive, or intransitive verb:one can move something, one can move oneself, and one can be moved. "Moving" can be an adjective, or a gerund (the process of carrying out the action represented by the verb "to move"). "Move" can be a noun, as when discussing actions in a chess game. "Moving" can refer to translocation in space or to a particularly strong emotional shift. Living creatures move (excepting dormant viruses or bacteria):movement can be considered an essential (but not sufficient) characteristic of a living being. This one verb, in its many forms and meanings, covers a lot of life.

I have devoted much of my scientific career to the study of animals moving in the course of goal-directed activities. Like all of us, I have derived strong satisfaction throughout my life from moving myself and objects:in recreational activities (that includes sports and games), in solving problems and in household activities, like caring for children (lots of movement involved in that!), gardening, cooking, crafts projects of all kinds, and home repairs. It seems natural to me to ask how and why we humans and other creatures move and what role moving plays in our respective lives. Here, I track the arc of my career over four decades studying goal-directed movement, mainly in platyrrhine monkeys. I have other interests, too, but in the service of brevity, I won't mention these.

Revisiting old projects might be of historical interest, but in this essay I have another purpose for doing so. I hope to illustrate for early-career researchers how a satisfying, to me exciting, long-running research program grew by asking (usually) simple questions, persisting when things did not turn out as planned, embracing different approaches, and joining in collaboration with others. I hope this essay will spark ideas for early-career primatologists/comparative psychologists/ethologists as they set out building their own careers. "Things are different now," but that was also true when I began my career in research in the mid-1970s. "Things" are always changing (moving, of course).

I have organized the essay in seven roughly chronological sections. The first two sections are about the beginning: they concern my first research projects as a graduate student with squirrel and titi monkeys, through a postdoctoral field project, and when establishing my own laboratory with capuchin monkeys. I had no preconceived ideas about how my career would develop in these periods:I was simply looking for opportunities and following them as best I could when they appeared. Sections 3 and 4 concern observational studies of spontaneous manual activity and its development in captive capuchin monkeys, and experimental studies of the monkeys' hand movements while grasping and handling objects. These topics seemed the obvious starting points to link studies with captive monkeys to their behavioral biology, building upon my observations of wild capuchin monkeys. Section 5 concerns studies of how captive capuchin monkeys combined objects into stable structures. These studies explored how capuchin monkeys managed tasks that in the human developmental literature were interpreted as reflecting particular cognitive abilities that were considered beyond what nonhuman primates achieved. The monkeys' performance on these tasks bolstered my growing engagement with embodied explanations of skilled actions. Section 6 addresses laboratory studies of monkeys using objects to probe, hammer, and rake other objects to achieve a goal (in my terminology, tooling:Fragaszy & Mangalam, ). These studies linked capuchin's propensity to combine objects, a propensity that in my understanding is related to foraging, exploration, and other routine daily activities, and therefore must be understood as part of an animal's behavioral biology. Section 7 concerns studies of wild monkeys using stones to crack nuts, a fascinating phenomenon that our research team brought to scientific attention about 20 years ago. It might appear from the (retrospectively constructed) logical topical progression laid out in this article that the final portion of my research career was pre-ordained from its beginnings, but that is certainly false. Instead, my career grew organically, with a strong dose of serendipity. Read on to see one version of how it happened.

First, a brief explanation about how I got into primatology: Throughout my childhood, I cared for animals (principally dogs, sheep, horses, and chickens) on our family's farm. I spent many hours watching animals, including females during birth and mothers with newborns. Our sheep sometimes rejected their newborn lambs, leading to exhaustive efforts to cross-foster the lambs. At university, for my class in Comparative Psychology, I wrote a term paper about how mammals came to bond with their young and what supported or impeded cross-fostering. Despite diligent search, I found no literature about this topic in sheep, but I found many articles about bonding between baby monkeys and their biological or foster mothers. At the same time as I was writing about maternal and filial bonding, I volunteered as a research assistant in Dr. Peter Klopfer's project examining maternal care in lemurs. I loved the experience. Applying for graduate school, these interests led me to programs where I could study maternal care and infant development in monkeys. Thus I came to primatology, via lambs and lemurs.
INITIAL EXPLORATIONS: MOVING ONESELF THROUGH THE LANDSCAPE

I began my graduate research career in Dr. W. A. (Bill) Mason's laboratory at the California Primate Research Center (CPRC), University of California, Davis, in 1973, working with five pairs each of pair-housed squirrel monkeys (Saimiri sciureus) and titi monkeys (identified as Callicebus moloch at the time; more recently, as Plecturocebus cupreus  1 ). These monkeys were not involved in other studies when I arrived at the CPRC, so I had the freedom (and encouragement from Dr. Mason) to initiate my own studies. My first task was to get to know the monkeys, as I had never seen a monkey in person before arriving at the laboratory. To that end, I watched them in their home cages as they explored novel objects (Fragaszy & Mason, ) and as they fed (Fragaszy & Mason, ). I saw that titi monkeys remained near one another, and they acted together in time and space, whereas squirrel monkeys moved and acted independently and were generally more active. I interpreted these differences as supporting each species' typical grouping and use of space in natural settings as known at that time:squirrel monkeys in large groups with relatively loose coordination among group members and large home ranges, and titi monkeys in monogamous family groups that moved together in small territories. I was fascinated that their species-typical behaviors across different situations:choosing and eating food, interacting with partners, exploring novel situations:fit together so coherently.

For my dissertation research, I chose to test the general idea that the pronounced behavioral differences between squirrel monkeys and titi monkeys that I had documented in my observational studies reflected deeply-rooted organizational tendencies that would be manifest across many dimensions of behavior. I wanted to test the idea in larger spaces than the monkeys' home cages, so that the monkeys would have greater agency to organize their travel and to use space in some measure like they could in natural settings. I was aiming for ecological validity. To this end, I undertook studies using an outdoor enclosure much larger than the monkeys' home enclosures (Fragaszy, , ). With the help of CPRC staff, who had better construction skills than I did, we constructed a starting area, goal box, and adjustable long runways in the outdoor enclosure (Supporting Information: Figures S1-S3), and I conducted a set of three related experiments on individual monkeys' travel along the experimental pathways to the goal box, which contained food on one side and the pair mate on the other (Figures 1 and 2). Conducting these experiments provided a valuable lesson for me as a novice researcher, even more so than the logistically simpler observational studies I had completed. The lesson is that one should wade bravely into new ways of doing things:you can (and will need to) develop new skills to pursue your own ideas. Do not expect that your research site will have exactly what you need to conduct the study you want. Expect to create those conditions yourself. It is a liberating experience.

Testing squirrel and tii monkeys' movements along experimental pathways in an outdoor enclosure, reported in Fragaszy. This photo shows the start area and the experimenters' viewing window. The monkey was released from its carry box at the center front edge of the start area to move onto the experimental pathways. Photo by D. Fragaszy.

Testing squirrel and tii monkeys' movements along experimental pathways in an outdoor enclosure, reported in Fragaszy. This photo shows the last segment of the route to the goal box, which contained food on one side and the pairmate on the other. Photo by D. Fragaszy.

The three experiments investigated the monkeys' travel to a goal location when the visual, physical, and spatial properties of the paths varied systematically. These experiments revealed that the squirrel and titi monkeys differed strongly in their interest in traveling on novel versus familiar pathways, and in how they behaved in the process of choosing a route. Squirrel monkeys traveled readily along novel routes, including along new shortcuts, but also more often traveled to the end of a dead-end path than did titi monkeys, with apparently little regard for how far they traveled. These characteristics support persistent travel and foraging in large areas. Titi monkeys took longer to pass the choice point, especially if the layout of possible routes had changed. They often took the familiar route even when they passed shorter routes to the goal while traveling on the familiar (longer) route. These characteristics support efficient travel in a familiar home range.

The magnitude of the difference between the species in their travel preferences along the constructed routes so impressed me that I wanted to examine the monkeys' behavior in an even larger space that more closely approximated spaces wild monkeys would inhabit. Fortunately for this plan, a one-hectare space fully enclosed with wire mesh rising to 10 m above the ground had just been built at the CPRC, expressly for the purpose of establishing a small naturalistic enclosure for platyrrhine monkeys. Before monkeys were placed in the enclosure on a permanent basis, I was permitted to use it for experiments featuring releasing a pair of monkeys into the enclosure for 1 h at a time. The enclosure had been planted with fruit trees, but these were under 1.5 m and did not provide continuous routes through the enclosure, so once again I undertook construction of above-ground pathways, and an observation platform 10 m away from the nearest runway (Figure 3). The experimental design featured releasing a pair of monkeys together onto a complex runway system containing six boxes baited with preferred foods ("foraging stations") in a space mostly planted in sunflowers (Figure 4; Fragaszy, ). The goal was to examine the monkeys' travel along the runways to the various foraging stations over the 1-h period. At the end of the hour, we invited the monkeys to enter their familiar travel boxes (in which they had traveled to the enclosure) for the ride home. Each pair was released into the enclosure five times. I predicted the titi monkeys would travel together and move systematically along the runways to visit the foraging stations. I predicted the squirrel monkeys would travel more independently, travel farther, and exploit the foraging stations in a less systematic manner than the titi monkeys. I further expected the monkeys of both species to enter willingly their travel boxes at the end of their hour-long exploration of this novel space, and fortunately, this expectation was met.

Squirrel and titi monkeys' movements in a 1 ha enclosure. Schematic of above-ground runway system, six foraging stations, and observer platform. Pairs of monkeys were released into the enclosure, each pair for five 1-h periods. See Fragaszy. Photo by D. Fragaszy.

Squirrel and titi monkeys' movements in a 1 ha enclosure. A foraging station on a runway system in the enclosure, with a squirrel monkey sitting on its roof eating provisions from the station. See Fragaszy. Photo by D. Fragaszy.

The monkeys had not read my proposal, however. They did not restrict their travel to the above-ground paths we had laboriously constructed for them, and they never visited all the foraging stations in a given hour. Fortunately, though, they did many other interesting things that bore on the questions I had in mind when I designed the study. So, instead of analyzing the monkeys' movements along travel paths to predetermined destinations (foraging stations), I pivoted to analyzing their movements and use of space in the entire enclosure. And in this full space, the monkeys did largely adhere to the patterns I observed in the smaller runway system used in the previous experiment. Titi pairmates generally followed one another, were in contact for a larger proportion of the time, used a small portion of the overall space, developed strong preferences for particular spaces, and moved shorter distances and for less time than squirrel monkeys. They also used the provided runways more than the squirrel monkeys, and fed primarily at the feeding stations. Squirrel monkeys traveled independently of each other, traveled mainly away from the feeding stations, and spent more time traveling than titi monkeys. The differences in how monkeys of each species organized their movements through large spaces were robust and large, and fit into the larger pattern of how monkeys of each species lived their lives in natural settings. And I learned to keep my eye on the big picture question and to make the most of the unexpected findings from a "failed" experiment (i.e., an experiment where the monkeys did something completely different from what I expected).
MOVING ON IN MY CAREER: GETTING TO KNOW CAPUCHINS

After earning my PhD. in 1978, I graduated into the wide world of research and academia outside of the CPRC and University of California (UC) Davis. I hoped to obtain a faculty position and to establish my own laboratory program with captive monkeys (I had a backup plan as well, in case that did not pan out:faculty positions for comparative psychologists have never been abundant, as far as I can tell). I hoped to establish a laboratory research program featuring capuchin monkeys that had a reputation as clever manipulators but had been little studied. Their apparent cleverness was fascinating to me. Moreover, I had read that they were relatively easy to keep in captivity, compared to the titi monkeys I studied at UC Davis, so that I could reasonably entertain the idea of caring for them properly in the absence of the highly experienced staff of the CPRC. I read everything about capuchin monkeys that I could, which included the reports of early European naturalists who had encountered captive capuchin monkeys and who reported the stories that indigenous people told them about the monkeys. Of course, at that point in my career, I had never seen a capuchin monkey in person. To be best prepared for this new project, I followed Dr. Mason's advice: I should know the natural behavior (i.e., behavior in natural environments) of any species I intended to study in the laboratory, so that I could interpret what I saw in relation to the species' lifestyle and ecology:an ethological approach. Accordingly, I used a 1-year postdoctoral fellowship from the National Science Foundation to study manual activity of wild capuchin monkeys. This project presented numerous opportunities (to discover something new, as wild capuchins of any species had been little studied at the time), challenges (learning different methods of observation and data analysis; working alone), and complicated logistics (living and working in a remote area). I was very fortunate to find a site (Hato Masaguaral, in the llanos of Venezuela) just suited to my goals, and even more fortunate that Dr. John Robinson, who had studied the capuchin monkeys at that site (Cebus olivaceus; at the time, Cebus nigrivitattus) for several years (Robinson, ), was on site when I arrived to help me learn to find and individually identify the monkeys, to find my way home again at the end of the day, and to provide tips on how to deal with the local complexities of flooded ground, bamboo thickets, and disappearing monkeys. John Robinson's help enabled me to use my relatively limited time at Masaguaral productively.

When I wrote my post-doctoral fellowship application, I was also applying for permanent faculty positions, and I was hired in the spring of 1979 as a tenure-track Assistant Professor of Psychology by San Diego State University (SDSU), to begin that fall. I was awarded the post-doctoral fellowship a few months later, just before I was supposed to begin my first year in my new faculty position. My department head suggested that I begin my faculty position and then take a 1-year leave of absence from my faculty position. Thus, I would have a home base and a job to return to at the end of my period in the field, and my university colleagues would get to know me before I left. My department head thought this was a better plan than accepting the faculty position and leaving for the field before beginning my teaching and faculty work, and I think he was right. The National Science Foundation approved a delayed start for my fellowship, and so I taught at SDSU for 1 year, and then went to Venezuela.

Observing monkeys conducting their daily lives in a natural setting was exhilarating for me. I was so caught up in following the monkeys, watching them, and recording what they did, particularly with their hands, in as much detail and as systematically as I could that I routinely forgot to eat lunch, despite having breakfasted lightly at 4:30 AM. Unlike me, the monkeys never forgot to eat. They spent nearly half of their daylight hours engaged in activities related to feeding. Most impressive to me was the great effort they devoted to biting, pulling, and pounding objects vigorously while foraging (Fragaszy, ). One of their most interesting activities was banging large snails against tree limbs to break them open. Adults were rather good at this, but juveniles were often unsuccessful, despite lengthy and vigorous sessions of banging. Monkeys of all ages commonly sifted through the debris that collected in the "boots" (broken fronds along the trunk) and crowns of palm trees, pulling out and eating wasps, ants, lizards, and countless small creatures that I could not identify before they disappeared into a monkey's mouth. I was surprised at how much time the monkeys spent on the ground playing, searching for food, and traveling (Fragaszy, , ; Fragaszy & Boinski, ), given that they are considered arboreal animals. I gained a strong appreciation for the can-do attitude of capuchin monkeys, their curiosity, and the diversity of their foraging activity. I also understood Bill Mason's insistence that knowing the behavior of your study species (or genus, in my case) in a natural environment is necessary for a biologically informed understanding of that species' behavior in captive settings.
Establishing a research program with captive capuchin monkeys

Before I left for my field project in the summer of 1980, on the advice of a friend I spoke with at an American Society of Primatologists meeting, I wrote to Dr. William London (whom I had never met), asking for a loan of tufted (robust) capuchin monkeys (Cebus apella at the time, Sapajus spp. now) from the colony that was under his care at the National Institutes of Health. In return, I offered to be responsible for the costs of their care at San Diego State University (an offer that my Dean had approved). In the spring of 1982, a year after I returned from Venezuela, Dr. London sent me 11 tufted capuchin monkeys (8 females and 3 males), which we housed together with squirrel monkeys (Saimiri sciureus) already at SDSU in two mixed-species groups in a facility constructed for that purpose. Together with an enthusiastic crew of students, we began to study the monkeys.
USING HANDS AND HANDLING OBJECTS: MANUAL ACTIVITY AND ITS DEVELOPMENT

I had seen in wedge-capped capuchins in Venezuela engage in vigorous manipulation very frequently and in many different forms. Several actions by wild monkeys involved combining objects and substrates (e.g., banging an object on a tree trunk). To know more about this aspect of their manual activity, we began by documenting how the monkeys behaved with and without various objects placed in their enclosure (Westergaard & Fragaszy, ). We showed how much more varied and frequent the monkeys' manual actions were when a straw substrate and varied objects were present:simple and expected findings, but an important starting point and a good means for us to become familiar with the monkeys' actions and to establish best husbandry practices. In this first study, we noted several unexpected behaviors, such as the capuchin monkeys readily using containers as cups and placing paper towels in containers they filled with water, making sponges that they then manipulated. These observations suggested how variable manipulative behavior could underlie capuchin monkeys' discovery of solutions to instrumental problems that were identified as capuchins' "cleverness" in popular understanding (such as escaping from locked cages).

Two studies completed in our first 2 years with the capuchin colony particularly influenced my research program. First, Michael Costello demonstrated that capuchin monkeys, but not squirrel monkeys, used precision grips to grasp small, stationary items (Costello & Fragaszy, ). Second, Greg Westergaard demonstrated that capuchin monkeys, but not squirrel monkeys, manufactured and used plant probes for "fishing" viscous syrup from an enclosed container (Westergaard & Fragaszy, ). At the time, the communities of primatologists studying manual function and tool use in nonhuman primates did not expect either of these findings in a platyrrhine monkey, so the findings opened new questions for me about capuching monkeys' dexterity.

In 1984, I moved with my colony of capuchin monkeys (and my human family as well!) to Washington State University. I turned my attention to the systematic study of spontaneous manual activity in our captive monkeys. Leah Adams-Curtis, my first PhD student, and I analyzed the frequency and variety of the monkeys' manipulative behavior (Fragaszy & Adams-Curtis, ). We were especially interested in behaviors involving combining an object with another object or surface, because of the potential value of such combinatorial actions to the monkeys' discovery of novel uses of objects. Adapting the ethogram that I had developed for coding manual actions in wild capuchins for our laboratory setting, we coded the manual actions of 31 capuchin monkeys of both sexes and all ages in two groups. The monkeys were housed in indoor enclosures with straw bedding and fresh branches from local vegetation (collectively, browse), and durable movable items attached to perches, walls, and ceiling, and we scattered small food items in the straw a few times each week, with the aim of providing diverse opportunities for locomotion and manipulation. A large glass window afforded a clear view into each enclosure. We collected data on focal animals for 10-min periods with pencil and paper in real time on time-lined check-sheets. To do so reliably, we used a semi-continuous method (5 s observing, 5 s recording), recording each unique combination of action and object(s) that was observed in a 5-sec period. We categorized the data into functional activities (Table 1) and also into categories defined by the relations among the body, the object(s), and the substrate (Table 2).

The high rate of manual activity expressed by the monkeys was the first striking finding. The second striking finding was the magnitude of the difference across ages in this rate. Juvenile monkeys (13-39 months old) acted with objects in 45% of intervals, more than twice the rate of adults or infants. Adults directed most of their actions towards food, infants towards exploring surfaces. Juveniles expressed most of their activity in variable manipulation. Monkeys of all ages occasionally combined loose objects with fixed objects or other (loose) objects or more often, with a surface of the enclosure. These relational actions composed a greater proportion of manual activity for juveniles than for adults or infants. Thus, several lines of evidence showed that juveniles were super-charged manipulators.

This study (Fragaszy & Adams-Curtis, ) demonstrated that capuchin monkeys produced considerable generativity in the variety of their actions with a single object, the variety of objects towards which they direct the same act, and the frequency and proportion of their actions that include an object and another object or surface (combinatorial actions). My interpretation is that capuchin monkeys' manipulative generativity enables them to discover the usefulness of novel actions with objects, as they produce such actions regularly.
Looking at the origins: manual development

In keeping with an ethological orientation, we aimed to understand the development of capuchins' unusual manipulative propensities. We first studied infant monkeys during the first 6 months of life (the period during which infants are largely dependent on a carrier), interpreting our findings in relation to the infants' motor capabilities, which change rapidly across this period (Adams-Curtis & Fragaszy,). Then, we studied young monkeys across the first 2 years (encompassing the period when monkeys gradually take on full responsibility for feeding themselves, during the second year) (Fragaszy & Adams-Curtis, ).

We divided the first 6 months into three 8-week periods, which corresponded to the developmental milestones of the onset of independent locomotion (by 8 weeks) and the appearance of vigorous manual actions (from 16 weeks). At birth, capuchin monkeys showed no manipulative activity beyond clinging to a carrier. For the first 8 weeks, young monkeys mostly looked at objects and surfaces near them, and reached towards them. If they touched them, they scratched, picked, tapped, licked, or sniffed them. They rarely grasped an object. In weeks 8-16, monkeys greatly increased the frequency of manipulative actions, and produced more actions that involved holding an object, although these actions still made up a minority of their actions. Their manual actions remained relatively imprecise and gentle. The changes between the first and second 8 weeks are probably related to an increase in the amount of time infants spent alert and active (Fragaszy, ), a decrease in the amount of time spent in a ventral position on the mother (a position which impedes access to objects and surfaces), improvements in postural stability and stamina, and the onset of independent locomotion, which allowed infants to approach items of interest to them. From 17 to 24 weeks, the frequency of manual actions doubled from that of the previous 8 weeks, and more vigorous or precise actions (hit/bang, push/pull, rub/roll, insert/extract, and handle) increased in frequency. The majority of the young capuchin monkeys in this study in Weeks 17 to 24 produced all the forms of manipulation seen in adults, although with less vigor, stamina, and precision than by adults. Subsequent research confirmed and extended this general picture for captive capuchin monkeys (Byrne & Suomi, ), and we may hope soon to have comparable data from wild monkeys. A longitudinal study of two infants, video recorded weekly for 30 min from Weeks 5 to 25 in our lab, revealed that bimanual actions appeared at the same time as unimanual actions, and complementary actions (in which each hand takes a different role) were observed as soon as manipulation began to be frequent, at 8 and 9 weeks (Adams-Curtis et al., ). In all, these studies established that infant capuchin monkeys display species-typical manipulation as soon as their postural abilities and stamina support these actions, and over time, actions become more differentiated and more precise.

Turning now to the longer view of development, between the first 6 months and the second 6 months, the trends continued that manipulation increased in frequency, in the proportion that was vigorous or required fine motor control, and in the proportion directed at portable objects. By 1 year of age, young monkeys displayed adult levels of stamina and fine motor control. They also enthusiastically engaged in vigorous and prolonged activity with available objects, especially combining them with available surfaces (e.g., banging, rubbing, pulling, inserting) and biting them. All these actions are prominent in foraging in natural settings. Capuchin monkeys typically are gradually weaned during their second year, as their permanent dentition appears, and they reach approximately half of adult body size. At this point, they are equipped physically and in terms of their action repertoire to feed on the same foods as adults (Chalk et al., ). Thereafter, increasing strength and specific knowledge probably contribute to improving foraging competence in young capuchins (Eadie, ; Gunst, Boinski, et al., ; Gunst, Leca, et al., , Laird et al., ).

These studies and others (Byrne & Suomi, ; Fragaszy,, , ) illustrated the variability across ages in the monkeys' manipulative behavior, and allowed me to view that variability in relation to other behavioral domains (postural stability, locomotor abilities, state regulation), their life history and their behavioral ecology. Although I did not know it at the time, this broad understanding would be invaluable to our later studies of how young monkeys acquire the unlikely skills of using objects as tools, and most notably, large stones to crack nuts.
MOVING HANDS: MANUAL DEXTERITY

Michael Costello's findings (Costello & Fragaszy, ) had shown that capuchin monkeys could oppose thumb and index fingers to achieve a form of precision grip, a finding extended and refined by Spinozzi et al.  and neuroscientists interested in mapping the neurological correlates of these actions (e.g., Mayer et al., ). Note that capuchin monkeys also display versatile grips in several other forms (e.g., Truppa et al., , ); we must be mindful not to over-rate the importance of one particular posture of the hand to these monkeys' manual dexterity. In collaboration with Marianne Christel and her students, we sought to understand in more detail how and when capuchin monkeys used precision grips. For this purpose, we analyzed precisely calibrated video of capuchin monkeys in my lab grasping small objects placed in shallow grooves (Christel & Fragaszy, ). These analyses showed that capuchin monkeys placed one or more fingers in lateral opposition to the thumb when picking up small items but that such grips were effortful for them, taking longer and more often failing than when using all fingers in opposition. In this sense, capuchin monkeys use their hands very differently than do catarrhine monkeys, that preferentially use precision grips to grasp small objects.

However, the tasks we had presented to the monkeys to that point in time did not entice them to use their hands in all the ways I had seen capuchin monkeys do as they foraged in natural settings. As Jones and Lederman explain, humans use their hands for haptic perception, exploration, and other non-prehensile purposes (such as gesturing) throughout life. These aspects of manual function have received far less attention by comparative psychologists and biologists than prehension. Thus, Agnes Lacreuse and I (Lacreuse & Fragaszy, ) broadened our studies to aspects of manual function beyond grips. We showed that capuchins used exploratory movements with their hands when searching for hidden food items that were similar to humans' exploratory movements (Lederman & Klatzky, ), suggesting continuity across primates in this aspect of manual function. I also wanted to know if capuchin monkeys used compound grips, as Macfarlane and Graziano had described for macaques (M. mulatta), to hold multiple objects in one hand, and in-hand movements to move objects, using the synergistic movements of the fingers that Elliott and Connolly described as typical of humans. Creating tasks that would naturally elicit such movements, if the monkeys could produce them, in laboratory settings where we could see them was an unmet challenge. To examine synergistic digital movements, Jessica Crast observed capuchin monkeys in our lab aligning small objects to pass through a matching cut-out in a vertical panel (Crast, ). The monkeys occasionally used simple synergies (simultaneous use of the digits in convergent flexion) and reciprocal synergies (combinations of movements in which the thumb moves differently than the other digits, as in rolling an object between thumb and other digits) to do so, but not sequential synergies (in which the thumb moves in a dissimilar or reciprocating way from the other digits, as when turning a pen from end to end). Mainly capuchin monkeys relied on whole-hand manipulations to move the small objects to and through the aperture, pressing the object into the palm, then sliding it across the panel until it passed through the aperture (Supporting Information: Figure S4). We also created a task that seems promising for eliciting compound grips and related movements of the hand: we invited the monkeys to drop small balls into a tube to receive a food reward. By encouraging them to use one hand to drop two or more balls into the tube, we enticed them to handle multiple objects dynamically in one hand (Figure 5; Jones & Fragaszy, ). The monkeys showed us a new side of their dexterity in these studies. In general, I hope that primatologists direct more attention to hand movements. My hunch is that we will discover unexpected variability (e.g., in tarsiers; Fragaszy & Crast, ).
