MOVING OBJECTS TO SOLVE INSTRUMENTAL PROBLEMS IN THE LABORATORY

In 1990 I moved, with human family and capuchin monkey colony, to the University of Georgia to take up the faculty position in the Psychology Department that I still hold (since May 2019, as Emerita status). Soon after, as part of a new collaboration with colleagues at the Language Research Center (LRC), Georgia State University, we were inspired to challenge the monkeys in my laboratory and the apes at the LRC with an instrumental task drawn from Greenfield et al.'s study of human children combining cups into a seriated set. Creating sets of cups is an engaging activity for human children, and we thought it could be a feasible and engaging task for nonhuman primates to illuminate combinatorial actions. Greenfield et al. showed that children aged 36 months and older, but not younger children, would preferentially place one cup inside another, then place that pair inside a third, larger cup, a strategy they called "subassembly." Using this strategy was associated with consistent success at seriating five cups, and success at inserting a sixth cup into the middle of the set, which required partially deconstructing the seriated set and reconstructing it including the additional cup. Children younger than 36 months were more likely to use two other strategies when trying to create a five-cup set: pairing one cup with one other ("pairing"), but not proceeding to a larger structure, and adding one cup to a set of cups ("potting"). If pursued with cups in descending order by size, potting can result in a seriated set. However, young children typically do not select cups strictly in order by size, and they generally failed to seriate the cups if they used only this strategy (see also DeLoache et al., ). Greenfield later drew on the 1972 study to support her argument that parallels existed between children's development of grammatical language (combining words into units that are then embedded in longer units, in specific sequences) and rule-guided manual activity, including their emerging use of objects as tools (combining objects in specific sequences) before they are 2 years old.

We wondered if nonhuman species would use rule-guided manual actions, including subassembly, when faced with the challenge of constructing a seriated set of cups, and if so, if this form of combining cups would confer greater success in the task and in solving the additional problem of inserting a sixth cup after seriating a set of five cups, as it did for human children. Julie Johnson-Pynn, Elizabeth Hirsch, Karen Brakke, Patricia Greenfield, and I aimed to find out (Johnson-Pynn et al., ). Some of the apes at the Language Research Center had had training in the use of human language, and some had been reared in a conversational context with human caretakers (Savage-Rumbaugh et al., ), adding further richness to the comparisons in which we were interested. We replicated in part Greenfield et al.'s (1972) procedure: the experimenter first seriated five cups using subassembly as the subject watched, and then the subject was given the cups to handle. If the subject constructed a seriated set of five cups, it was given a sixth cup to insert into the middle of the set.

This study produced several unexpected and compelling findings, among them, that monkeys and apes were similarly proficient at seriating sets of five cups and both groups used potting and subassembly to do so in equal proportions. Most subjects of each group succeeded at inserting a sixth cup into a five-cup set they had just constructed. In short, three species of nonhuman primates, some with and some without language training, performed equally on this task and some did so in a manner similar to 3-year-old children. We concluded that although the hierarchical combination of words into sentences may be organized in the same way as objects are combined into structures, any shared underlying process is phylogenetically more widely distributed than language.

To explain the development of combinatorial skills in young children in the seriation task in terms of cognitive processes unique to humans, one must demonstrate that young children move from an inability to seriate to success at seriation in some manner that is different from the way that nonhumans manage the same challenge. To put this hypothesis to the test, we extended our study to include 11-, 16-, and 21-month-old children (12 of each age group) to compare the earliest emergence of seriation in humans with our findings from nonhuman primates. The children decreased pairing and increased potting cups with increasing age, but children of all ages rarely used subassembly. Fifteen of the children created one or more seriated sets of five cups, but only 2 of the 15 children correctly inserted the sixth cup into the set, once each. Capuchin monkeys and apes, in comparison, seriated all five cups on more than half of their trials, and they frequently succeeded at inserting the sixth cup into the seriated five-cup set. When inserting a sixth cup, both children and the nonhuman primates used subassembly more often than they had used it to create the five-cup set. These findings support Greenfield et al.'s (1972) proposal that subassembly reflects emerging mastery in this task. However, we argued that using subassembly does not reflect a qualitatively different combinatorial strategy. Instead, we proposed that "the participants' behavior reflects experientially driven increases in the forms of activity that constrain the degrees of freedom to be managed in the task." (Fragaszy et al., , p. 128).

We continued to explore these ideas in three experiments with six capuchin monkeys in our laboratory, two of which had not participated in the previous experiment (Rosengart & Fragaszy, ). In the first experiment, with the two new monkeys, we looked at the way the monkey's success and use of combinatorial procedures to seriate a set of five cups changed with experience. The monkeys improved their success at seriating cups with experience, as expected, and at the same time, they increased the number of moves used per seriation event. Thus, rather than learning to seriate the cups more efficiently, they learned to persevere at the task. Even unsystematically combining cups will eventually result in a seriated set, so perseverance pays off. In Experiment 2, we gave six monkeys same-sized cups that could be combined in any order to form a stable structure. Some individuals used one procedure more than others, indicating that the monkeys were not randomly using combinatorial procedures, and their preferences were stronger with the same-sized cups than they had been when the monkeys worked with the variably-sized cups in the earlier study (Johnson-Pynn et al., ). Finally, in Experiment 3, two monkeys that exhibited a consistent preference for potting with the seriating set of cups in the 1999 study were explicitly trained to use the subassembly procedure with a new set of cups. They were then retested with the same seriating set of five cups used in the 1999 study. Both monkeys' use of subassembly was greater in Experiment 3 than it was in the 1999 study. In all three experiments, altering the context and the individual's experience altered the monkeys' combinatorial actions.

The findings from these several studies of monkeys, apes, and young children working with seriating cups increased my interest in embodied theories of behavior, stemming from ecological psychology as presented by Gibson,  and elaborated and integrated with dynamical systems theory (e.g., Chemero, ; Richardson et al., ; Thelen & Smith, ; Witt & Riley, ). It took me about 20 years from the time I completed my PhD to the time I found and understood a theoretical position (or more properly, a family of theories) that fit with my intuitive understanding of behavioral flexibility as reflecting concurrent organismic, environmental, and task-dependent elements. The ecological, embedded/embodied perspective has informed my work for the last 20-plus years.

A series of studies illustrates how we brought an ecological approach to another task that involved inserting one object into another:placing an object into a matching cut-out in a surface, like a children's wooden form puzzle (Supporting Information: Figure S5). The first two studies in the series were conducted in collaboration with Charles Menzel and included chimpanzees at the LRC (Fragaszy et al., ; LaCour et al., ). We showed that capuchins and chimpanzees had equally great difficulty aligning an object with more than one axis (such as a T-shaped object) into a matching cutout, and that they aligned even a straight stick with a matching cutout imprecisely. They appeared to use primarily haptic cues to fit the stick into the cutout, sliding the stick along the surface of the tray until it slipped into the cutout. Neither group could work with two planar dimensions concurrently. In these aspects of behavior, they differed dramatically from children as young as 2 years working on the same problem (Fragaszy et al., ). These fundamental differences in the way that humans and nonhuman primates perceive and act with objects and surfaces, we argued, must contribute to humans' tremendous advantage in using hand tools. A nonhuman primate would have great difficulty using a screwdriver, for example, because it would have difficulty inserting the tip into the slot of the screw head. Appreciating nonhuman primates' capabilities in this domain allows refinement of our ideas about what kinds of hand tools nonhuman primates might use, and the perceptuomotor processes supporting humans' tooling.
TOOLING IN THE LABORATORY

Within a year of establishing a laboratory with capuchin monkeys, we had shown that captive capuchin monkeys would manufacture probes from available browse and use them to collect food from an enclosed container (Westergaard & Fragaszy, ). In 1984 I attended the Congress of the International Primatological Society and heard Elisabetta Visalberghi speak about a capuchin monkey at the Rome zoo using a stone to smash food items (Visalberghi & Antinucci, ). We talked at length about our complementary findings and decided that we should collaborate to understand when, how, and why capuchin monkeys used objects as tools. We began our collaboration in 1986 with a joint study of capuchin monkeys solving new problems using objects. We invented two devices, one that required probing and one that required hammering, and presented them to the two groups of monkeys in my laboratory. Some monkeys mastered each of these devices (Fragaszy & Visalberghi, ). Most monkeys observed with interest the actions of others at the devices, but we saw no evidence that any monkey learned how to solve the problems (use a probe or a hammer) from observing others. This conclusion contradicted widespread ideas at the time that monkeys learned novel behaviors from one another, as suggested by the example of Japanese monkeys at Koshima washing sweet potatoes (Kawai, ). We proposed instead that monkeys' (and other animals') learning was influenced by social partners in other ways, such as by enhanced interest in a particular object or location or by restricted access to such locations, and that individuals learned by their own actions how to solve a problem (Fragaszy & Visalberghi,, ; Visalberghi & Fragaszy, , ). Later, we showed that even indirect social contributions to learning can powerfully affect (particularly young) monkeys learning to solve an instrumental problem, and support traditional skills in a group (Crast et al., ).

About a decade later, Sarah Cummins-Sebree and I undertook studies of individual monkeys using objects of various shapes and materials as tools and moving objects across irregular surfaces. We situated this work explicitly in the Gibsonian ecological framework (Gibson, , ), informed by Lockman's insightful paper framing development of tool use in human children as a process of perceptual learning supported by species-typical exploratory routines. We interpreted monkeys' behavior with tools in varied situations in terms of their perception of affordances (Jones, ). Examples of these studies include using hooks of different shapes and materials to pull something within reach across a solid or irregular surface (Cummins-Sebree & Fragaszy, , ) (Figures 6 and 7), and using a hoe with a jointed handle to pull something within reach (Fragaszy et al., ). Several other studies along these lines remain to be written up, a task that I hope to complete. In all these studies, the ecological, embodied perception-action perspective led us to examine how monkeys moved and used objects, rather than what they knew or understood about "tools," as manifest in their choice of an object before using it, which was and remains an alternative approach to studying cognitive processes involved in tooling (Osuna-Mascaro et al., ; Visalberghi et al., ).

TOOLING IN NATURE: ETHOCEBUS PROJECT

In early 2003, Stephen Nash shared an article from BBC Wildlife, written and illustrated by photographer Peter Oxford, with me, Linda Fedigan, and Elisabetta Visalberghi. Stephen was thinking about capuchin monkeys a lot at that time, as he provided several illustrations for the book about capuchin monkeys that Elisabetta, Linda, and I were completing (Fragaszy et al., ). I will be forever grateful that he thought to send us that article. The article included photos of a purportedly wild robust capuchin monkey standing upright and using an enormous stone to crack a palm nut on a stone anvil, with an accompanying text claiming that capuchin monkeys in this area cracked nuts in this way on a regular basis. Elisabetta and I knew immediately that we must find this population and see for ourselves what these monkeys were doing (Linda had her hands full at her own field site in Santa Rosa National Park, Costa Rica). In early September 2003, together with Patricia Izar from the University of Sao Paulo, we first stepped into the rural landscape of rocky cliffs and open woodland at Fazenda Boa Vista, Piaui, Brazil. In the course of our short initial visit (5 days!) we confirmed, with the help of the landowner M. Oliveira, that these monkeys were truly wild, and that most adults did crack nuts using large stones (Figure 8). Moreover, we documented on that first visit that the monkeys used anvils in many places in their home range, suggesting that cracking nuts was a common behavior among these monkeys (Fragaszy, Izar et al.,). Armed with these preliminary findings, with nearly an infinite number of questions to answer about these monkeys and their unusual behavior, and with the landowners' gracious permission to conduct research on their property, we obtained funding to conduct research at the site. We returned in January 2005 to start the EthoCebus project (https://www.ip.usp.br/site/ethocebus/ethocebus/) 2  ,  3  (Visalberghi & Fragaszy, ). The EthoCebus project includes wide-ranging ethological and ecological investigations, and the participation of a large number of people: local residents, students, and collaborators in geography, geology, archaeology, anthropology, and human kinesiology, and affiliated with institutions in Brazil, Italy, and USA. Our findings from the project have provided a unique platyrrhine reference point for discussions about behavioral and ecological correlates of tooling by wild primates and ancestral hominins (e.g., Visalberghi et al., ). The monkeys at the site have become widely known within the nature documentary community (and thus, among the general public) as "rock stars" for their impressive skills, appearing, for example, in the BBC program "One Life" and in "Monkeys: An Amazing Animal Family," produced by Offspring Films.
A bearded capuchin monkey at the EthoCebus field site uses a stone hammer and anvil to crack palm nuts, with two juvenile observers close at hand. Photo courtesy of Barth Wright.

I focus here on those portions of the EthoCebus project in which I have had the most involvement and in which movement of individuals was a central concern. These include experimental studies concerning how monkeys detected affordances for transporting stones and cracking nuts, kinematic studies of the monkeys' movements during these episodes to analyze the nature of their skilled actions, and observational studies of young monkeys' developing expertise. Our experimental studies of the monkeys' behavior around anvil sites (selecting and transporting stones to crack nuts; selecting nuts; selecting anvils; handling nuts and stones at anvils before striking, actions with the stone while striking nuts) have been, I think, particularly productive, and I hope their success will inspire others to adopt similar techniques in their work. My and Elisabetta's many years of conducting ethologically grounded experiments with group-housed capuchin monkeys, apes, and humans provided us with an experimental mindset that we brought to the EthoCebus project, and an ecological/embodied approach led to (I thought obvious) starting points for investigations of their unusual skills. The experimental studies took place in a relatively flat, open area containing several anvil sites encircled by large trees. These anvils had been used on a regular basis by the monkeys since before our arrival. The landscape in that area lends itself to unobstructed observation and video recording. We established that monkeys cracked several species of locally abundant nuts using stones weighing on average close to 1 kg (Spagnoletti et al., ), a relatively heavy stone for monkeys weighing 1.9-4.4 kg as adults (Fragaszy et al., ). They cracked a nut with a few to more than 70 strikes (Fragaszy et al., ), indicating a wide range of skill.
Choosing stones and nuts

In our initial experiments, Elisabetta was particularly interested in how selectively the monkeys chose materials. I was interested in how, through movement, the monkeys used their senses as perceptual systems, echoing the title of J. J. Gibson's classic book (Gibson, ), and in the features of their skill. Using artificially manufactured stones, we showed that when presented with a set of stones, the monkeys identified the most effective combination of mass and composition for cracking palm nuts (Visalberghi et al., ), even when the ratio of the mass of the two stones approached 1:1 and the stones were of equivalent volume, shape, and material (Fragaszy, Greenberg et al., ) (Figure 9). Before choosing stones, the monkeys tapped and handled them. Monkeys showed similarly closely titrated choices among pairs of stones of different mass set at different distances to the closest anvil (Massaro et al., ). They preferred to crack the least resistant nut first, when two nuts of varying resistance were present (Fragaszy et al., ). When given the choice of experimentally prepared anvils with pits of systematically varying dimensions, the monkeys explored the pits indirectly by placing a nut in the pit and then striking the nut with a stone. They preferred pits in which they cracked nuts with the fewest strikes, although their preferences for pits were weaker than their preferences for nuts or stones (Liu et al., ). We suggested they could develop stronger preferences for stones and nuts because they handled hese objects directly, whereas they contacted the pits indirectly with the nut or the stone. These studies highlighted how monkeys explored stones, nuts, and anvils using haptic and kinesthetic senses to detect affordances and organize actions.

A bearded capuchin monkey handling one of two manufactured stones that have equal volume but unequal mass, before choosing the heavier one to crack the nut on the anvil. See Fragaszy et al., . Photo courtesy of Rebecca Greenberg.
Transporting stones:bipedal locomotion while carrying a load

Bearded capuchin monkeys typically carry hammer stones bipedally. Nonhuman primates transporting a load bipedally serve as comparative reference points to those concerned with the evolution of bipedalism in hominins, but observations of wild nonhuman primates spontaneously transporting a load bipedally are extremely rare. We took advantage of our opportunities to study this phenomenon (Duarte et al. 2012) (Figure 10). First we established the parameters of the monkeys' locomotion while carrying a load and compared them with those of capuchins in the laboratory walking bipedally without carrying a load (Demes, ), concluding that the variable in which load-carrying bipedalism appears to differ from unloaded bipedalism in capuchins occurs at the ankle and specifically at toe-off, where the foot leaves the ground surface to initiate a stride.

Bearded capuchin monkeys transport hammer stones bipedally. A view of the experimental area across which the monkeys transported a stone and a nut on the way to an anvil (off view to the right). The monkeys typically carried the stone and nut in a straight line from the pick-up location to the anvil. Notice the erect posture of the monkeys' trunk, despite its bent-hip, bent-knee mode of locomotion. See Duarte et al. (2012) and Hanna et al.. Photo courtesy of Rebecca Greenberg.

Next, we measured ground forces during bipedal transports (Hanna et al., ). This required instrumenting the path along which the monkeys traveled to the anvil with a force plate in a manner compatible with the monkeys moving across it. We buried a portable force plate (Figure S6) so that the platform was level with the ground surface, then placed a stone where a monkey would be likely to carry it directly over the force plate to a preferred anvil. This seemingly aspirational set-up worked surprisingly well. We recorded spatiotemporal and force data for all three components of the ground reaction force for 28 bipedal steps. We confirmed that capuchins exhibited a mean vertical peak force per total weight (Vpk) for the hindlimb consistent with those of unloaded capuchins in the laboratory and for other bipedal primates, including humans, and laterally (outward) directed medio-lateral forces, presumably to stabilize side-to-side movements of the center of mass. Unexpectedly, vertical force traces exhibited a measurable spike in vertical force at foot contact ("impact spike") in 85% of the steps recorded. An impact spike is common in force recordings of humans walking and running, and is thought to be a source of injury and degeneration in the lower limb (Lieberman et al., ) but the phenomenon had not been reported for other primates. Once again capuchin monkeys provide an interesting comparison with hominins.
Handling nuts

Observation of how monkeys cracked nuts led us to additional studies focused on exploratory actions. For example, we noted that the monkeys consistently put the nut into an existing pit in the anvil to strike it. Further, we noticed that the monkeys frequently tapped the nut on the edge or interior of the pit repeatedly before releasing it and turning their attention to the stone, and that they rotated and turned stones before lifting them to crack. From an ecological perspective, these actions were probably directed toward exploring affordances haptically. To explore this possibility, we evaluated how the monkeys handled nuts in the course of setting them in the anvil, and the relation between these actions and the properties of the nuts (mass, size, shape) of one species of palm (Fragaszy, Liu, et al., ). We measured the shape of the nuts by rolling them on a flat concrete surface and marking the meridian where the nut stopped rolling with a line, so that we could see where the "stop" meridian was located when the monkey placed the nut in a pit. The monkeys consistently placed the stop meridian facing skyward, regardless of mass and size of the nut. Next, we asked people to mark what they judged to be the center of the most symmetrical part of an unmarked nut. When we rolled the nut on the floor to find the stop meridian, they had marked the symmetrical center as the stop meridian. Thus, we concluded that the monkeys, through tapping the nut in the pit, routinely placed the nut with the more symmetrical sides of the nut facing the vertical edges of the pit. The position of the nut in the pit affects how force travels through the shell of the nut when it is struck by the stone, thus affecting how and where the shell cracks and how the nut rebounds from the strike. Further work is needed to evaluate exactly how positioning the nut in this way promotes effective cracking, but my intuition is that it reduces the rebound of the nut, making it less likely that the nut flies off the anvil. Losing the nut from rebound after the strike is a common poor outcome of a strike for monkeys of all ages and levels of expertise.
Handling stones

We noticed that after they had arrived at an anvil and placed the nut in a stable position, the monkeys often lifted, flipped, or rotated the hammer stone a few times, placing the hands in different positions, before lifting it to strike the nut. These actions seemed likely sources of information for monkeys preparing to use the stone. We also noticed that sometimes monkeys moved one or both hands from the side(s) of the stone to its top during the strike, suggesting they finely tuned moving their hands with movement of the stone. To investigate how often the monkeys moved their hands and stones in these ways, we presented monkeys with unfamiliar stones and nuts to crack. Four monkeys proficient at cracking nuts used two stones of relatively lower mass (455 and 524 g) and two of relatively higher mass (1042 and 1100 g) (Fragaszy, Morrow et al., ) to crack highly resistant nuts (piacava; Orbygnia spp.) routinely cracked by these monkeys. The monkeys spun and flipped the larger stones more often than the smaller stones, and they performed what we labeled preparatory lifts more often with the larger stones. Next, we presented piacava nuts and less resistant nuts (tucum, Astrocaryum spp.) with an unfamiliar 1042 g stone. Twelve monkeys participated in this study, producing on average 0.9 exploratory actions per strike in their first 20 strikes with this stone. Most monkeys gripped the stone on the sides and moved one or both hands to the top on over 90% of their strikes. One monkey, however, lifted the stone with one hand on the bottom and one on the side on 11 of his 20 strikes, and kept his hand on the bottom of the stone on two of these strikes. Unsurprisingly, he achieved rather poor outcomes, dropping the stone off the anvil on more than a third of his strikes and causing the nut to fly off the anvil on nearly half of his strikes. In contrast, a monkey missing one foot, so that he stood on one leg to lift the stone, always moved one or both hands to the top of the stone on the downward portion of his strikes, and dropped the stone off the anvil just once. Skill matters.

We extended our investigation to how young monkeys handled stones, comparing the actions of six young monkeys (2-5 years old, 1.2-2.0 kg) and six adult monkeys (1.9-4.2 kg) using a small stone (540 g) to crack tucum nuts that are relatively easy to crack (Fragaszy et al., ). Juveniles, like adults, rarely struck the nut with a slanting trajectory or missed the nut or lost control of the stone after a strike. Juveniles used a more diverse set of exploratory actions than adults, as one would expect given that they were learning how to manage gripping and moving a hammer stone. They also less frequently moved their hands from the side of the stone to the top during the strike, an indication that the manner in which adults dynamically adjust their grip on the stone during the strike is a finely tuned skill.

Our close examination of how monkeys worked with nuts and with stones during cracking reinforced our impressions that these monkeys work carefully to achieve specific outcomes when they start an episode of cracking nuts. Choices matter, and actions matter. The monkeys attend carefully to both, and proficient choices and actions reflect expertise acquired through extensive practice.
Characterizing expertise

A different kind of analysis, drawn from observations of monkeys outside of experimental situations, affords further insight how long it takes for young monkeys to acquire expertise at this strenuous activity (Fragaszy, Aempichitkijkarn, et al., ) (Videos 1, 2 and 3). We sampled the behavior across the day of 16 young capuchin monkeys ranging in age from 3 months to 6.3 years over five observation cycles at 6-month intervals, and the behavior of seven adults in one of those cycles. The study's broad aims included analyzing the social context in which young monkeys learned to crack nuts (Eshchar et al., ; Fragaszy, Eshchar, et al., ), but for this analysis we focused exclusively on bouts of nut-cracking, analyzing the relations among behaviors that reflected young monkeys' learning about affordances through practice, their body mass, and their effectiveness at cracking nuts. We could include body mass in the analysis because we have longitudinal records of body mass for the individuals in our main study group from 2007 through 2016, collected with a scale mounted in a tree at the outdoor laboratory with a bowl of water at one edge of the scale as enticement for the monkeys to come there (Fragaszy et al.,  (Figure 11), a method that I hope others can use as well. Body mass is a key indicator of growth and health, and an enormously useful variable in developmental analyses. The adults cracked the nut on 74% or more of their bouts of cracking, and we classed them as Experts. Intermediates cracked nuts in up to 43% of bouts, and Novices cracked no nuts, despite striking nuts with stones. All monkeys that cracked nuts weighed at least 1.4 kg, suggesting a lower limit of mass for effective management of coordinating movement of the body +  stone system, but among Intermediates, neither age nor body mass strongly correlated with success at cracking nuts. Instead, compared to novices, monkeys with intermediate skill spent more time trying to crack a nut in a given bout, lower rates of striking a nut directly on the anvil, higher rates of positioning the nut on the anvil, and higher proportions of actions devoted to positioning the nut on the anvil, out of all actions with the nut and stone before and between strikes. Experts differed from intermediates in the same direction, except that their bouts of striking a nut with a stone were much shorter than intermediates' and more likely to end in cracking the nut. The intermediates individually displayed greater variability than novices or experts across bouts in bout duration and in rates of positioning and striking. These findings supported our conception of nut-cracking as a learned skill that requires practice to master, rather than a behavior that is enabled by increasing body mass, and our impression that intermediates are more likely than novices or experts to vary their behavior from one bout to the next. Video 1 illustrates a novice, Video 2 an intermediate, and Video 3 an expert during a bout of nut-cracking. The differences among the three individuals in how they handle the stone and the nut are obvious.

Movement of the body + stone system in nut-cracking

The final embodied aspect of cracking nuts that I will address is the kinematics of movement of the body + stone system during striking. To understand how monkeys control the trajectory of a large hammer stone held in their hands during rapid lifting and lowering while standing upright, I undertook studies with Qing Liu and Madhur Mangalam using kinesiological methods.

One has to record movement over time through a calibrated space to evaluate its kinematics. Daily, we created a two-dimensional calibrated space by recording a 1-m square frame, with reflective tape at the corners and at measured distances between the corners, centered on the long axis of the log and the pit in its center. When the calibration process was complete, we placed one or more stones near the anvil and a few nuts. We filmed monkeys opportunistically as they came to the anvil and cracked nuts. Later, from frame-by-frame video playback, we manually coded the x-y coordinates of the calibration frame, and then of anatomical markers (ear, wrist, elbow, shoulder, etc.) for the monkey across all frames per strike to create a model of the motion of the body and the stone during the strike (Supporting Information: Figure S7).

We first showed that the monkeys lifted the hammer stone to about chest height, or 60% of body length, then lowered it by flexing at the hips, knees, and ankles (Liu et al., ). The entire strike (lifting and lowering) lasted about 3/4 of a second. Monkeys proficient at cracking produced hammer trajectories to strike nuts with highly repeatable spatial profiles, even when the mass of the stone varied nearly four-fold, between 0.5 and 1.9 kg (Liu et al., ; Mangalam et al., ; Mangalam, Pacheco, et al., ). They regulated the kinematic parameters of each strike to some degree as a function of the condition of the nut when cracking relatively soft Astrocaryum (tucum) nuts that have a fibrous husk surrounding the kernel (Mangalam & Fragaszy, ; Mangalam et al., ). Compared to human experts (that had about 40 times the body mass of the monkeys, not to mention longer arms) cracking the same species of nuts using the same stones on the same anvil, the monkeys added less work to the stones, varied the work added across stones of different masses, and used more strikes to crack the nuts. However, the expert monkeys used fewer strikes to open the nut than did novice human nut-crackers (Mangalam et al., ; see also Fragaszy et al., ), indicating once again that the monkeys had refined their skill at this task. Overall, monkeys regulated amplitude and velocity of the stone within a narrow range, regardless of the mass of the stone or the species of nut they cracked. Maintaining a consistent amplitude and velocity of the stone is supported by synergies of movement across joints, particularly of the foot and lower leg, indicating the importance of stable bipedal balance in skilled striking with a stone (Mangalam, Pacheco, et al., ; Mangalam, Rein, et al., ). The kinematic markers of monkeys' skill at cracking nuts are as clear as the categorical markers we identified using ethological methods.

The corpus of work we have completed to date on the kinematics of nut-cracking in bearded capuchins highlights the embodied character of this skill. When one understands the importance of dynamic balance and the tight control of the trajectory of the stone, evident in the tight synergies of movement across joints, to effective performance, coupled with the physical constraints of the monkeys' size and strength, one can appreciate why it takes monkeys years to acquire their full skill at cracking palm nuts. Working to understand the character of this skill with a hand tool, so rare among nonhuman animals and so reminiscent of percussive tool use by ancestral hominins, from as many perspectives and with as many colleagues from different disciplines as I could manage has been highly rewarding. It has opened up new questions about skill in other creatures using objects as tools (tooling, in our terminology: Fragaszy & Mangalam, ). Together with Madhur Mangalam, I have been developing a theory of tooling that permits predictions about where and how nonhuman species will tool, bringing tooling into biology (Colbourne et al., ; Fragaszy & Mangalam,, ; Mangalam & Fragaszy, ; Mangalam, et al.,) and tooling in nonhumans into psychology (Arbib et al., ; Mangalam et al., ). Exciting times indeed!
CONCLUDING REMARKS 4

In keeping with the aim of the Founders Symposium that was the source of this special section, I want to mention for junior scientists the importance of participation in professional societies:in the case of primatologists, that includes national or regional primatological societies (such as the American Society of Primatologists, ASP) and our global society (the International Primatological Society, IPS). Many of you know that I served as President of both ASP and IPS, and before that I served on the Council of the IPS in several different roles. I took the time from my other professional and academic tasks for these service positions because I believe strongly that every scientist has a responsibility to support science in the most general sense, as it is a societal good. There are also benefits to each of us from participating, as those of you who are active in a professional society no doubt know first-hand. Supporting collaborations, mentoring junior scientists, speaking for the discipline to governments and interest groups:IPS and ASP are great places for primatologists to carry out these important professional responsibilities. Primatology is recognized by the general public as a valuable branch of science that contributes to society. Let us work together to build on the public's confidence in us. Envision what you want your scientific discipline to be for the good of the animals we study, for ourselves and our colleagues, and for society at large, and then work to realize that vision.

I was asked to mention how I balanced career, particularly time in the field, with family obligations. Every person's story of meeting this challenge will be different, but perhaps familiarity with case studies can help young scientists think about how they can find balance. There are three key answers in my case. First, my husband has always supported my decisions about career and travel, and together we navigated the difficult "two body problem" (two careers, but seeking one home location) with generally good success. Second, my mother-in-law lived with us from the time our first child was born, and she too supported my decisions. A multi-generational family meant that I could work away from home for varying periods with little disruption to the family's routines when our three children were young. This does not mean it was easy for me, but I did not feel that my family suffered as a result. There were always two adults at home. I am deeply grateful to Elizabeth Fragaszy for this gift of time. My field work in Brazil began when our children were grown and thus my time away from home was simpler to organize. Third, I jealously guarded most evenings and all holidays and school vacations as family time. I strongly believe that taking appropriate time away from work enhanced my productivity at work.

passages.text: Optimizing acute stroke treatment process: insights from sub-tasks durations in a prospective observational time and motion study
Background

Rapid treatment is critical in managing acute ischemic stroke (AIS) to improve patient outcomes. Various strategies have been used to optimize this treatment process, including the Acute Stroke Protocol (ASP) activation, and minimizing the duration of key performance metrices, such as door-to-needle time (DNT), CT-to-needle time (CTNT), CT-to-groin puncture time (CTGP), and door-to-groin puncture time (DGPT). However, identifying the delay-causing sub-tasks within the ASP could yield novel insights, facilitating optimization strategies for the AIS treatment process.
Methods

This two-phase prospective observational time and motion study aimed to identify sub-tasks and compare their respective durations involved in the treatment process for AIS patients within ASPs. The study compared sub-task durations between "routine working hours" and "evenings and weekends" (after-hours), as well as between stroke neurologists and non-stroke neurologists. Additionally, the established performance metrices of AIS were compared among the aforementioned groups.
Results

Phase 1 identified and categorized 34 sub-tasks into five broad categories, while Phase 2 analyzed the ASP for 389 patients. Among the 185 patients included in the study, 57 received revascularization treatment, with 30 receiving intravenous (IV) thrombolysis only, 20 receiving endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) only, and 7 receiving both IV thrombolysis and EVT. Significant delays were observed in sub-tasks including triage, registration, patient history sharing, treatment decisions, preparation of patients, preparation of thrombolytic agents, and angiosuite preparation. The majority of these significant delays (P < 0.05) were observed when were performed by a non-stroke neurologist and during after-hours operations. Furthermore, certain sub-tasks were exclusively performed during after-hours or when the treatment was provided by a non-stroke neurologist. Consequently, DNT, CTNT, and CTGP were significantly prolonged for both non-stroke neurologists and off-hours treatment. DGPT was significantly longer only when the ASP was conducted by non-stroke neurologists.
Conclusions

The study identified several sub-tasks that lead to significant delays during the execution of the ASP. These findings provide a premise to design targeted quality improvement interventions to optimize the ASP for these specific delay-causing sub-tasks, particularly for non-stroke neurologists and after-hours. This approach has the potential to significantly enhance the efficiency of the AIS treatment process.
1. Introduction

Providing rapid and efficient treatment is crucial for managing acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and improving patient outcomes. Quality improvement studies in AIS have focused on identifying, establishing, and improving key process indices, including door-to-CT (DTCT), door-to-needle time (DNT), CT-to-needle time (CTNT), CT-to-groin puncture time (CTGP), and door-to-groin puncture time (DGPT). These indices serve as benchmarks for evaluating and optimizing the efficiency of an Acute Stoke Protocol (ASP) to ensure optimal numbers of patients have good outcomes. The Canadian Best Practice Recommendations for Acute Stroke recommend DNT and DGPT benchmarks of 30 and 60 minutes, respectively. Significant efforts to improve the treatment process of AIS has been made in Canada and other parts of the world. However, the AIS treatment process is inherently intricate and multifaceted, involving numerous interdependent processes and clinical specialties. This intricate composition makes the process susceptible to potential delays, necessitating a continuous pursuit of optimization to ensure the achievement of optimal patient outcomes.

A novel approach could be to break-down the AIS treatment process into smaller steps, which we will refer to as "sub-tasks". In healthcare, no formal definition for "sub-tasks" exists, but they can be seen as small, specific actions or components within a larger task or process. These sub-tasks contribute to the overall completion of the task and can be identified, measured, and optimized to make the process more efficient. Within the context of the AIS treatment process, key tasks that is used in studies aimed to lower treatment times include DTCT, CTNT, and CTGP times. These tasks can then be broken down into smaller tasks (sub-tasks) such as patient triage, registration, blood sample collection, sharing medical history, neurological evaluation, and transport to the radiology department, among others. The approach of identifying sub-tasks and quantifying their durations, followed by the identification of sub-tasks resulting in delays may provide valuable insights into the AIS treatment process, which may inform new improvement strategies and ultimately lead to better patient outcomes.

Observational "time and motion study" is a method from industrial engineering that may aid in identifying and documenting sub-tasks and their durations. This method involves observing and measuring tasks within a process using a stopwatch to establish the corresponding times for the sub-tasks. Observational time and motion studies have previously been utilized to enhance overall emergency department (ED) workflow and minimize wait times. However, its application in optimizing the AIS treatment process remains unexplored.

The objectives of this study encompassed three main aspects. Firstly, it aimed to identify sub-tasks involved in the AIS treatment process. Secondly, it measured and recorded the durations of these sub-tasks to further determine potential sub-tasks causing treatment delays. This objective involved comparing sub-task durations between "routine working hours" and "evenings and weekends" (after-hours), as well as between stroke neurologists and non-stroke neurologists. Finally, the study aimed to assess the impact of these delay-causing sub-tasks on key process metrices of the ASP process, such as DNT and DGPT, among the abovementioned groups.
2. Materials and methods

A two-phase prospective observational time and motion study was undertaken to evaluate the AIS treatment process. The research protocol of this study received an exemption from the Nova Scotia Health Authority Research Ethical Board due to its focus on quality improvement. Instead, the study was approved by the Nova Scotia Health Authority Quality Improvement and Safety Council. Since the study was a quality improvement initiative and did not collect patient-level data, consent was not required from patients or their next of kin, either in written or verbal form.
2.1. Study center and population

The study was conducted in the Emergency Department (ED) at the Queen Elizabeth II Health Science Center (QEII) in Halifax, Nova Scotia (NS), Canada. QEII is the only comprehensive stroke center in the province of Nova Scotia. This hospital offers intravenous (IV) thrombolysis treatment to patients within its catchment area and provides endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) treatment to patients residing in the provinces of NS and Prince Edward Island (PE). Both NS and PE are relatively small in terms of area and population, with NS having a population of one million and PEI having a population of 173,000. QEII is a large urban tertiary care teaching hospital. The center was staffed with two stroke neurologists and 19 non-stroke neurologists during the study period, and has 24/7 on-site CT (computed tomography) services, along with interventional neuroradiologists.

The study focused on adult patients who were presented at the ED with an acute suspected stroke, resulting in the activation of the ASP. The study included only patients who had ASP activation before their arrival. Patients who had an in-hospital stroke and those who arrived within 10 min of pre-notification were not eligible. These exclusions were due to the unavailability of the on-site observer, who had to reach the location after receiving the pre-notification. The patient population encompassed those with ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), or stroke mimic.
2.2. Standard acute stroke treatment process at the study center

The AIS treatment process begins with the ASP activation by either the attending neurologist or the ED charge physician, either before or after the patient's ED arrival. A multidisciplinary stroke team, including a neurologist, neurology resident, stroke nurse (during routine hours), CT technician, and radiologist/radiology resident, is notified during this pre-notification period using a pager notification system. In the ED triage area, the patient is assessed by the ED nurse, neurologist, and neurology resident. Neurological examination, National Institutes of Health Stroke Score (NIHSS) assessment, and data collection from paramedics ensue.

The patient is then transported to the CT Scanner for brain imaging, starting with a plain CT head potentially followed by CT angiography (CTA), and CT perfusion (CTP). After imaging, patients may be further evaluated in the Diagnostic Radiology Department or the ED, depending on the neurologist's decision. Upon AIS confirmation, eligibility for IV thrombolysis and EVT is determined. While consent may be sought, emergency consent is typically applicable per Canadian guidelines. Treatment pathways vary based on IV thrombolysis, EVT, or both, and the time of day. During routine hours, IV thrombolysis occurs in the Radiology Department, while EVT patients await their turn in the Interventional Radiology Department angiosuite. After hours, patients return to the ED for IV thrombolysis and then proceed to the angiosuite for EVT, unless urgent issues necessitate ED treatment.
2.3. Observation and data collection phases

All patients were observed between 7 am and 11 pm, with "routine working hours" observations conducted on weekdays from 8 am to 4 pm, and all other observations considered during "after-hours". The rationale for considering the observation time from 7 am to 11 pm stemmed from the limited availability of the only observer, who meticulously documented the execution of each ASP.
2.3.1. Phase 1 observations to identify sub-tasks

In phase 1 of this study, conducted from November 1, 2021 to November 16, 2021, a single observer closely observed the AIS treatment process carried out by the stroke team. The observer, GK, is a Ph.D. candidate affiliated with a healthcare optimization laboratory dedicated to enhancing AIS treatment delivery. The observer aimed primarily to identify and document the sub-tasks within the AIS treatment process. Sub-tasks were identified based on reviews and opinions of stroke experts. Initially, five major tasks of the treatment process were defined based on the current literature: (1) Arrival to Imaging (Prior to Imaging), (2) Image Acquisition, (3) Treatment Decision, (4) Preparations for Thrombolysis, and (5) Preparation for EVT.
"Arrival to imaging" included the temporal duration from the suspected AIS patient's arrival at the ED to their transfer to the radiology department for imaging.
"Image acquisition" denoted the interval commencing upon arrival at the radiology department and culminating in the acquisition of CT imaging.
"Treatment decision" included the temporal duration between the acquisition of CT imaging and the determination to initiate thrombolytic therapy, based on CT imaging and AIS treatment guidelines.
"Preparations for thrombolysis" referred to the duration extending from the treatment decision to the actual administration of thrombolytic therapy.
"Preparation for EVT" signified the time elapsed from the administration of thrombolytic therapy to the initiation of groin puncture for the purpose of performing EVT.
Finally, in this phase of our study, sub-tasks carried out to complete each of these major tasks were meticulously identified and documented, relying upon the reviews and insights of stroke experts.
2.3.2. Phase 2 observations to measure and document the durations of sub-tasks

During the second observation phase:November 17, 2021 to June 15, 2022, the ASP workflow was closely monitored by the same observer to document all sub-tasks and their relevant information on a standard treatment process report form. The observer shadowed the workflow and recorded the following variables:
Mode of arrival: whether the patient arrived using EMS or as a walk-in.
Type of neurologist: if the ASP was conducted by a stroke neurologist or a non-stroke neurologist.
Time of day: whether the patient arrived during routine working hours or after-hours.
Diagnosis: determined after CT image acquisition, categorized as AIS, hemorrhage, stroke mimic, or unknown.
Treatment types: whether the patient received IV thrombolysis, EVT or both.
Start and end times of each sub-task: recorded for each suspected AIS patient.
If any new sub-tasks were observed during this phase, they were documented and recorded, along with any interruptions.
2.4. Outcomes

The outcome of the phase 1 study involved the identification and documentation of all the sub-tasks necessary to complete each major task within the ASP. The phase 2 study outcomes included differences in median durations of sub-tasks, comparing routine working hours with after-hours and stroke neurologists with non-stroke neurologists. Additionally, the study outcomes for the key process metrices of the ASP included differences in median durations of process metrices, including DTCT, CTNT, CTGP, DNT, and DTGP times.
2.5. Statistical analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to describe the baseline characteristics of the participants. Also, the baseline characteristics were compared between routine working hours and after-hours as well as between non-stroke neurologists and stroke neurologists, and the Chi-Square test was employed to analyze these categorical variables. Further, for each sub-task, the median duration and Interquartile Range (IQR) were calculated, and comparisons were made between the aforementioned groups using the Mann-Whitney U Test. Finally, the study also calculated the median DTCT, CTNT, CTGP, DNT, and DTGP time, with comparisons made between the above-mentioned groups using the Mann-Whitney U Test. These final comparisons were carried out to gain a comprehensive understanding of the effects of sub-tasks on the key process metrices of the ASP. The statistical analyses were conducted using Minitab version 21 (State College, PA).
3. Results
3.1. Phase 1
3.1.1. Observations to identify sub-tasks

During the phase 1 observational study, we identified the sub-tasks involved in the ASP guiding the treatment of AIS. Our observations led us to categorize the steps during ASP flow into five primary steps: Arrival to Imaging (Prior to Imaging), Image Acquisition, Treatment Decision, Preparations for Thrombolysis, and Preparation for EVT. We further classified the sub-tasks within each category based on their order of occurrence and location. In addition to the sub-tasks identified during Phase 1, some were also observed during Phase 2, resulting in a total of 34 sub-tasks related to ASP being recorded at the study center. Some sub-tasks were merged due to patient-related reasons, hospital staff-related factors, or study center-related constraints. This combining of sub-tasks was considered beneficial for assessment and comparison purposes.

3.2. Phase 2
3.2.1. Baseline characteristics of the observed patients and their treatment process

A total of 389 patients with suspected AIS and an ASP activation were assessed. Amongst them, 204 (52.4%) were excluded due to various reasons as mentioned in Figure 2. As a result, 185 (47.6%) patients with suspected AIS were observed during the study. Among the included patients, 106 (57.3%) arrived after-hours, 175 (94.6%) arrived by ground ambulance, 139 (75.1%) were assessed by a non-stroke neurologist, and 120 (64.9%) were diagnosed with stroke.
Flowchart of suspected acute stoke patients arrived with ASP activation.

Out of the 120 patients diagnosed with stroke, 93 (77.5%) had AIS, 14 (11.7%) had TIAs, and 13 (10.8%) had hemorrhagic strokes. Out of the 65 patients who did not have a stroke diagnosis, 3 (4.6%) were diagnosed with migraine, 5 (7.7%) were diagnosed with seizure, and 57 (87.7%) had an unclear diagnosis even after CT imaging; they were subsequently transferred to the ED for further assessment. Of the 93 patients diagnosed with ischemic stroke, 57 (61.3%) received treatment at the study center. The treatment modalities were distributed as follows among the treated patients: IV thrombolysis only (30 patients, 52.6%), EVT only (20 patients, 35.1%), and both IV thrombolysis and EVT (7 patients, 12.3%).

During the arrival to imaging stage, it was observed that sub-tasks "triage and registration" (median time in minutes, 2 vs. 4; U = 2,560.5; P = 0.049; Z = -1.97) took significantly longer time during off-hours, while sub-tasks "sharing patient's medical history" (median time in minutes, 1.5 vs. 2; U = 923.0; P = 0.038; Z = -2.07) took longer when the attending was a non-stroke neurologist. Conversely, during the image acquisition stage, none of the sub-tasks caused delays in treatment process, regardless of the time of day or the attending neurologist.

During the treatment decision stage, the sub-task "treatment decision time" took significantly longer both during off-hours (median time in minutes, 5 vs. 9; U = 228.0; P = 0.019; Z = -2.37) and when the ASP was carried out by a non-stroke neurologist (median time in minutes, 4.5 vs. 8; U = 188.5; P = 0.029; Z = -2.19). Further, the frequencies of sub-tasks "re-evaluation of the treatment decision," "consent conversation," and "laboratory results wait" were skewed toward non-stroke neurologists (88.9, 79.2, and 100.0%, respectively), and it was observed that stroke neurologists typically do not perform these sub-tasks. However, these sub-tasks did not reach a statistical significance due to them being performed in small numbers by stroke neurologists.

During the preparations for thrombolysis stage, the sub-task "preparing patient and mixing thrombolytic agent" took significantly longer both during off-hours (median time in minutes, 4 vs. 11; U = 76.0; P = 0.004; Z = -2.91) and when the attending was a non-stroke neurologist (median time in minutes, 3 vs. 8; U = 60.5; P = 0.010; Z = -2.57). Further, the sub-task "ED room arrangement" was exclusively observed during non-stroke neurologist treatment, and the majority (88.9%) of these arrangements occurred after-hours. Again, statistical significance cannot be established for this sub-task due to skewed distribution of the frequencies among the groups.

During the preparations for EVT stage, the sub-task "preparing angiosuite" took significantly longer both during off-hours (median time in minutes, 27.5 vs. 45; U = 24.5; P = 0.005; Z = -2.80) and when the attending was a non-stroke neurologist (median time in minutes, 27.5 vs. 43; U = 24.5; P = 0.011; Z = -2.54).
3.2.3. Comparison of the key process metrices of ASP process

In this study, the median times for overall key process metrices of the ASP process were determined. The median DTCT time was 14 min (IQR, 12-18.25), CTNT was 24 min (IQR, 14.5-35.5), DNT was 37 min (IQR, 29-50.5), CTGP time was 61.5 min (IQR, 52.5-91.25), and DTGP time was 74 min (IQR, 58-95). Further, group-wise comparisons of these process metrices were performed. For the routine working hours vs. after-hours comparisons, CTNT (median time in minutes, 15 vs. 27; U = 61.5; P < 0.001; Z = -3.33), DNT (median time in minutes, 30 vs. 42; U = 83.5; P = 0.008; Z = -2.66), and CTGP time (median time in minutes, 51.5 vs. 72; U = 35.5; P = 0.035; Z = -2.11) were significantly longer during after-hours. Similarly, CTNT (median time in minutes, 12.5 vs. 25; U = 55.5; P = 0.006; Z = -2.72), DNT (median time in minutes, 27 vs. 40; U = 56.5; P = 0.007; Z = -2.69), CTGP time (median time in minutes, 49.5 vs. 70; U = 21.5; P = 0.009; Z = -2.60), and DTGP time (median time in minutes, 59 vs. 83; U = 37.0; P = 0.038; Z = -2.07) were significantly longer when a non-stroke neurologist carried out the ASP. 4. Discussion

This study shows that applying an observational time and motion study to first identify and then quantify tasks has value in recognizing areas for improvement to reduce treatment time for AIS patients. Time and motion studies have been used in emergency departments to better understand workflow; however, time and motion study has not been applied to AIS treatment. The US Get With The Guidelines-Stroke registry collected whether specific predetermined delays occurred such as determining eligibility and hypertension control; however, the time spent on these tasks were not evaluated.

This study identified and quantified each specific task or sub-task in a single center, which is likely the most appropriate level to evaluate processes using time and motion studies. Each center often develops its own unique processes that are difficult to generalize across various centers. Therefore, the use of time and motion studies to identify areas for improvement can be extended to other individual centers, including smaller community and rural hospitals, which present distinct challenges, particularly concerning on-site resources and the need for tele-stroke services to make treatment decisions.

The results of this time and motion study showed that the study center had significant delays during off-hours. Poor patient outcomes and workflow delays during off-hours have been observed in EVT treatment. This study provides and reaffirms the occurrence of these delays during off-hours at the study center, affecting both thrombolysis and EVT treatment. Furthermore, this study highlights specific tasks contributing to treatment delays during off-hours, such as treatment decision-making, preparing patient and mixing the lytic drug, ED room arrangement before IV thrombolysis (89% occurrences during off-hours), and preparing the angiosuite.

Additionally, this time and motion study revealed that non-stroke neurologists performed additional non-value-added tasks and took longer task completion times in comparison to their stroke-trained colleagues. Specifically, non-stroke neurologists took longer in obtaining patient history and making treatment decisions. Further, specific sub-tasks, such as the re-evaluation of the treatment decision, consent conversation, laboratory results wait, and ED room arrangement, were either exclusively conducted or disproportionately performed by non-stroke neurologists, resulting in extended treatment times. This result is important, as there are currently very few studies that show that stroke trained neurologists perform more efficiently in the treatment of AIS patients. Challenges in the recruitment and retention of stroke neurology workforce has been identified, which is likely even more prevalent in the study setting of Nova Scotia, an economically constrained Canadian province with a small population. Furthermore, the study center is in a relatively small city of approximately 350,000 people in the urban center and 440,000 people in the larger metropolitan region. This presents challenges with relatively lower stroke volumes when compared to hospitals located in larger cities making resourcing of stroke neurologist even more challenging.

We believe that our study provides a frontier for future research aimed at improving the ASP process. Using our methodology as a foundation, stroke centers may identify their specific set of delay-causing sub-tasks at their respective facilities. Comprehensive stroke centers may utilize our approach to identify delay-causing sub-tasks in both IV thrombolysis and EVT treatment processes while primary stroke centers may focus on identifying optimization targets for IV thrombolysis at their centers. Based on their relevance and contextual conditions, potential strategies to optimize these delay-causing sub-tasks might include training sessions for efficient sub-task execution, parallel execution, or even considering the omission of certain non-value-adding sub-tasks.

Some limitations should be taken into consideration when interpreting the results of the current study. Firstly, it was not feasible to observe all patients arriving with an ASP activation, and the observations were limited to patients with an ETA exceeding 10 min. Additionally, the sample size was relatively small, which affected the observations for some sub-tasks that were recorded in low frequencies. Furthermore, the observations were limited to a specific time frame, from 7 am to 11 pm, and therefore, the sub-tasks identified in this study are limited to activities that occurred during the observation time frame. Finally, the study was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which imposed health regulations and restrictions that may have slightly affected the AIS treatment process.
5. Conclusions

The aim of the current study was to identify the sub-tasks that are associated with AIS treatment and determine their impact on the overall ASP process. The study center recorded several sub-tasks related to ASP, highlighting the complexity of the ASP process. During phase 2, the study identified multiple individual or combined sub-tasks that caused delays in the treatment process, both when a non-stroke neurologist was involved or when the ASP was carried out after-hours. Moreover, the study identified several sub-tasks that were exclusively performed during specific treatment situations. These delay-causing sub-tasks resulted in longer CTNT, DNT, and CTGP time for both non-stroke neurologists and after-hours ASPs. Furthermore, when a non-stroke neurologist conducted the ASP, the DTGP time was longer.

The study provides valuable insights into the sub-tasks associated with AIS treatment and their impact on the overall ASP process. Although there are some limitations, our study offers a distinctive approach by identifying areas of concern and subsequently designing targeted quality improvement interventions that could cater to the unique challenges of individual stroke centers. Further research is required to validate the findings in different settings and establish a foundation for the generalizability of targeted interventions aimed at reducing treatment delays.
